boundary_rationale: The book opens on its dated, located superscription — 'These are the words which Moses spoke to all Israel' (אֵ֣לֶּה הַדְּבָרִ֗ים אֲשֶׁ֨ר דִּבֶּ֤ר מֹשֶׁה֙ אֶל כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל) — but the record now has to reckon with 1:3, which the earlier draft passed over: a dated wayehi-formula (וַיְהִי֙ בְּאַרְבָּעִ֣ים שָׁנָ֔ה) attached to its own clause of the same verb, this time addressed אֶל בְּנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל rather than אֶל כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל. I read v.3 as the superscription's own internal date-stamp rather than a second speech-act: v.1 states the general fact and full addressee, v.3 supplies the calendar date on which that speaking occurred, using the identical verb because it is dating the same act. v.4 supplies a second dating clause of the same kind (after striking Sihon and Og), and v.5's הוֹאִ֣יל מֹשֶׁ֔ה בֵּאֵ֛ר אֶת הַתּוֹרָ֥ה הַזֹּ֖את לֵאמֹֽר remains the hinge handing off to the first-person quotation opening v.6. Nothing across vv.1-5 shifts to first person or changes the entity being described; the whole stretch functions as one composite, dated superscription. No petuchah or setumah exists anywhere in ch.1 to arbitrate the question, so this reading rests on text signal alone.
strongest_rejected_alternative: The stronger competing reading, now stated rather than omitted: split 1:1-2 | 1:3-5, treating v.3's dated דִּבֶּ֤ר מֹשֶׁה֙ אֶל בְּנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל as a second, independent speech-introduction parallel to v.1's, matching the granularity applied to the bare imperative cluster at 2:24 and the addressee-narrowing charge at 3:21. I subordinate it because both clauses remain third-person narration about the same act of Moses speaking to the same people on the same occasion — unlike 2:24 (a fresh imperative addressed to the people themselves) or 3:21 (a charge to a newly named individual) — but the case for treating v.3 as its own unit is real enough that a future pass could reasonably go the other way.

boundary_rationale: Moses’s quoted speech opens on its own recalled divine-speech formula, “Yahweh our God spoke to us in Horeb, saying” (יְהוָה אֱלֹהֵינוּ דִּבֶּר אֵלֵינוּ בְּחֹרֵב לֵאמֹר), a fresh embedded quotation distinct from the superscription that precedes it.
strongest_rejected_alternative: One could keep vv.6-18 together as one long recital of the Horeb-to-Kadesh period, but v.9 opens its own new topic (leadership) with its own “I spoke to you at that time” formula, so the departure command proper closes at v.8.

boundary_rationale: A fresh recital formula, 'I spoke to you at that time, saying, I am not able to bear you myself alone' (וָאֹמַ֣ר אֲלֵכֶ֔ם בָּעֵ֥ת הַהִ֖וא לֵאמֹ֑ר), opens Moses's own proposal to appoint tribal leaders. The people's assent at v.14 (וַֽתַּעֲנ֖וּ אֹתִ֑י וַתֹּ֣אמְר֔וּ טֽוֹב הַדָּבָ֥ר) uses the same answer-formula the draft credits as unit-opening at 1:22 and 1:41, but here it is a one-clause response accepting the proposal in the very sentence that made it, with no intervening turn — unlike the initiating requests at 1:22 and 1:41, which open new scenes the people themselves set in motion. The unit closes on the actual appointment act in v.15, before a narrower addressee (judges specifically) is charged with its own formula in v.16.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A reviewer applying the answer-formula mechanically could split 1:9-13 | 1:14-15 to match the granularity credited at 1:22 and 1:41; I decline because v.14 answers, rather than opens, the very proposal it follows — an assent embedded in its own antecedent rather than a fresh initiative, the distinction the earlier record left unstated.

boundary_rationale: Yahweh’s own sworn speech opens this unit with its own hearing-and-swearing formula, “Yahweh heard the voice of your words and was angry, and swore, saying” (וַיִּשְׁמַע יְהוָה אֶת קוֹל דִּבְרֵיכֶם וַיִּקְצֹף וַיִּשָּׁבַע לֵאמֹר), covering the excluded generation, the Caleb and Joshua exceptions, and the children’s inheritance, closing before the people’s own answering speech opens v.41.

boundary_rationale: The doomed-attack scene at 1:41-46 runs in unbroken second-plural narration -- וַֽתַּעֲנ֣וּ וַתֹּאמְר֣וּ, וַתַּמְרוּ֙, וַתָּזִ֖דוּ, וַתַּעֲל֥וּ, וַתֵּשְׁב֥וּ -- closing with 'you dwelt in Kadesh many days' (וַתֵּשְׁב֥וּ בְקָדֵ֖שׁ יָמִ֣ים רַבִּ֑ים כַּיָּמִ֖ים אֲשֶׁ֥ר יְשַׁבְתֶּֽם). 2:1 restates the same duration phrase at its own close -- 'you circled Mount Seir many days' (וַנֵּ֜פֶן וַנִּסַּ֤ע הַמִּדְבָּ֨רָה֙ דֶּ֣רֶךְ יַם ס֔וּף כַּאֲשֶׁ֛ר דִּבֶּ֥ר יְהוָ֖ה אֵלָ֑י וַנָּ֥סָב אֶת הַר שֵׂעִ֖יר יָמִ֥ים רַבִּֽים) -- but both instances of יָמִים רַבִּים are verse-final, so the repetition is a catchword linking two successive stage-closes rather than an inclusio, which would require the phrase to frame a unit from one edge to the other; nothing here is bracketed. Crossing the seam this decision draws also crosses a real person shift: 1:41-46 addresses the audience in the second plural throughout, and 2:1 switches without remark to first-plural narration, וַנֵּ֜פֶן וַנִּסַּ֤ע ... וַנָּ֥סָב. That shift is disclosed here as counter-evidence rather than absorbed silently. The span is kept at 1:41-2:1 because the catchword still binds the two verses more tightly to each other than either binds to its own chapter-internal neighbors, and the first paragraph mark in the book -- a samekh -- falls only after 2:1, corroborating (not driving) that the wandering notice belongs together through the end of 2:1. Given a real person-shift running against a catchword repetition that is not the inclusio it was called, confidence is lowered from high to medium.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Cutting at 1:46 and letting 2:1 open the next decision was reconsidered directly because of the 2mp/1cp shift: 1:41-46 never leaves the second plural, so a boundary drawn on person alone would fall exactly at 1:46|2:1. It is not adopted here because the catchword repetition of יָמִים רַבִּים and the samekh after 2:1 still bind 2:1 to 1:46 more strongly than 2:1 binds forward to 2:2's fresh divine-speech formula; but the alternative is close enough, and the person shift real enough, that the merge no longer supports high confidence.

boundary_rationale: The command proper opens on a bare, verse-length divine-speech formula, 'Yahweh said to me, saying' (וַיֹּ֥אמֶר יְהוָ֖ה אֵלַ֥י לֵאמֹֽר), the same construction the draft already treats as unit-opening at 2:9, 2:17, and 2:31 later in this chapter. It follows directly on the samekh closing 2:1 — the itinerary notice of turning and circling Seir now belongs with 1:41-46's scene as its shared-phrase close (see M8-Deut-009) rather than serving as this unit's own opener — and the command runs through the compliance report to its close in v.8, before a fresh Moab-directed command opens v.9 on the same formula.
strongest_rejected_alternative: One could keep 2:1 as this unit's opener on the strength of its itinerary verb וַנֵּ֜פֶן, which recurs at 3:1 to open the Og campaign. I decline: that verb's recurrence shows it can mark a fresh stage of travel, but here the samekh at the end of 2:1 and the repeated יָמִים רַבִּים binding 2:1 to 1:46 both argue that this occurrence closes the preceding stay at Kadesh rather than opening the Edom command, which has its own unambiguous formula one verse later.

boundary_rationale: Yahweh's self-declaration, 'I am Yahweh your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt' (אָֽנֹכִי֙ יְהוָ֣ה אֱלֹהֶ֔יךָ אֲשֶׁ֧ר הוֹצֵאתִ֛יךָ מֵאֶ֥רֶץ מִצְרַ֖יִם מִבֵּ֥ית עֲבָדִֽים), is grammatically declarative — a predicate-nominal clause identifying the speaker — set against every command from v.7 onward, each an apodictic prohibition built on לֹא plus the imperfect. That mood contrast is a genuine register signal internal to the Hebrew, not the WEB paragraph break the original entry leaned on, which is inadmissible under this campaign's own rule. Disclosed honestly: the Masoretic tradition does not corroborate this cut — no mark falls after 5:6 or after 5:7, and the next samekh is two verses later, after 5:10, so MT positively binds 5:6-10 as one closed section, running against rather than for this isolate. Low confidence reflects that the register signal is real but stands against, not with, the paragraph tradition.
strongest_rejected_alternative: MT's own section division argues for merging v.6 forward into 5:6-10 as one unbroken unit closed by the samekh after v.10, treating the self-declaration as the Decalogue's shared preamble rather than a decision-sized unit of its own. I keep the isolate provisionally because the declarative-versus-apodictic mood shift is a real text-internal signal, admissible on its own terms, independent of any paragraph mark; but the case for merging is the stronger one on Masoretic grounds, and the low confidence rating is meant to say so.

oshb:Deut.5.7 לֹ֥א יִהְיֶ֥ה לְךָ֛ אֱלֹהִ֥ים אֲחֵרִ֖ים עַל פָּנָֽיַ
parashah_two_witness: no pe/samekh after Deut.5.6 or Deut.5.7; samekh after Deut.5.10 (MT binds 5.6-10 as one section)

boundary_rationale: 'You shall have no other gods before me' (לֹ֥א יִהְיֶ֥ה לְךָ֛ אֱלֹהִ֥ים אֲחֵרִ֖ים עַל פָּנָֽיַ) is kept as its own decision on the strength of the traditional Decalogue enumeration, not any signal internal to this verse or corroborated by the Masoretic paragraphing. Checked directly against v.8, the two prohibitions share identical syntax (לֹא + imperfect + לְךָ), which argues against, not for, a register break between them; and no pe or samekh falls anywhere between 5:6 and 5:10, so MT does not mark this join either. The isolate survives here only as a record of the reception-tradition convention of ten discrete commandments, disclosed as such rather than dressed up as a textual seam.
strongest_rejected_alternative: The stronger reading merges v.7 forward with v.8 (or further, to the samekh at 5:10), since both are unelaborated apodictic prohibitions bound by identical syntax and by the absence of any Masoretic mark between them. I keep the traditional one-command isolate only because the campaign's working unit here is tracking the received Decalogue enumeration, and I flag plainly that this is a convention being followed, not a boundary the Hebrew text or its paragraph tradition supplies.

strongest_rejected_alternative: One could split the prohibition (v.8) from its rationale (vv.9-10) as two decisions, but the rationale’s “for I, Yahweh your God, am a jealous God” is syntactically the grounding clause for the very prohibition it follows, not an independent statement.

strongest_rejected_alternative: A reviewer might group this with the following murder/adultery/theft series as the start of the interpersonal commands, but its own elaborating rationale clause (“that your days may be long”) matches the pattern of the first-table commands rather than the unelaborated one-clause prohibitions that follow it.

boundary_rationale: Five commands run in series -- murder, adultery, theft, false witness, and coveting -- bound together not by a uniform bare-לֹא register, which the text does not actually exhibit, but by a waw-coordination chain: only 5:17 is asyndetic (לֹ֖א תִּרְצָֽח); every command from 5:18 through 5:21 opens with וְלֹא, syntactically coordinating each new prohibition back to the series 5:17 begins, a feature of this Deuteronomic Decalogue not shared by the asyndetic Exodus recension. That coordination is a genuine text-internal signal for treating the five as one continuous unit rather than an artifact of formatting. Set against it, disclosed rather than suppressed: a samekh follows each of 5:17, 5:18, 5:19, 5:20 and 5:21 individually -- five section marks, one after every command in the series, with no doubled mark at 5:21 recorded in the two-witness file (oshb_count and uxlc_count both 135, no duplicate sites) -- converging with (though not driven by) WEB's own separate editorial paragraphing of the same five commands. This is not the densest cluster of paragraph marks in the book: the twelve-curse liturgy at 27:14-27:25 carries a samekh after every one of its twelve verses in succession, closed by a petuchah at 27:26, a longer and more strongly corroborated run than the five here. The coordination-chain reading is kept, but at low confidence, because the Masoretic tradition's own witness runs the other way at every internal seam.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A five-way split, one decision per command, is fully defensible and arguably better corroborated: each command carries its own setumah, and each is a distinct legal topic (murder is not theft). I do not adopt it because the waw-chain binding 18-21 back to 17 is a real syntactic feature the split would sever, treating five grammatically coordinated clauses as five independent sentences when the Hebrew does not read that way. Both readings have genuine textual support; this is recorded as the closest call in the block, resolved toward the merge only because the coordination is a positive text signal and not merely the absence of one.

boundary_rationale: The Shema itself opens on Deuteronomy’s most concentrated confessional formula, “Hear, Israel: Yahweh is our God. Yahweh is one” (שְׁמַע יִשְׂרָאֵל יְהוָה אֱלֹהֵינוּ יְהוָה אֶחָד), extending through the love-command and its household-transmission instructions (teaching children, hand, frontlets, doorposts), closing before a fresh warning-conditional opens v.10.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A reviewer could separate the confession-plus-love-command (vv.4-5) from the transmission instructions (vv.6-9), but v.6’s “These words…shall be on your heart” is the direct antecedent “these words” refers to, binding the transmission instructions to the command they transmit.

boundary_rationale: A fresh conditional opens on 'It shall be, when Yahweh your God brings you into the land' (וְהָיָ֞ה כִּ֥י יְבִיאֲךָ֣ יְהוָ֣ה אֱלֹהֶ֗יךָ אֶל הָאָ֜רֶץ), the book's recurring prosperity-amnesia pattern, following directly on the samekh that closes the Shema unit at 6:9. The span now runs through the beware-lest-you-forget caution (v.12), the fear-and-serve command (v.13), and the jealous-God warning (v.15), closing on the samekh that falls at the end of 6:15 — one of a run of four section marks across this stretch of the chapter (6:9, 6:15, 6:19, 6:25) that the earlier 6:13 cut never engaged. Nothing marks a discourse turn at 6:13 itself: no vocative, no presentative, no fresh imperative-of-remembering, only a continuation of the same second-person warning chain 6:10 already opened. The real internal seam in this stretch sits one verse later, at the Massah prohibition opening 6:16 (see M8-Deut-043).
strongest_rejected_alternative: The original cut placed the boundary at 6:13, on the strength of a fronted-object construction treated as opening a fresh positive command. Checked against the samekh pattern across 6:9-25, that fronting is real but corresponds to no Masoretic division, while the samekh after 6:15 does; the fronted object reads more naturally as continuing the same warning-and-exhortation register that began at 6:10 (fear, serve, swear — all responses to the same forgetting-danger) than as opening independent content.

boundary_rationale: A fresh prohibition opens the unit, 'You shall not test Yahweh your God, as you tested him in Massah' (לֹ֣א תְנַסּ֔וּ אֶת יְהוָ֖ה אֱלֹהֵיכֶ֑ם כַּאֲשֶׁ֥ר נִסִּיתֶ֖ם בַּמַּסָּֽה), naming a specific past failure by name — a fresh case, not a continuation of the fear-serve-swear exhortation that precedes it — and following directly on the samekh closing 6:15. It runs through the renewed command to keep the commandments diligently (v.17) and the do-what-is-right formula (v.18) to the dispossession promise closing v.19, where a further samekh corroborates the stop before the catechetical unit opens fresh at v.20.
strongest_rejected_alternative: The original span opened at 6:13 on the fear-and-serve command; I decline to keep that edge because nothing there marks a fresh turn, while 6:16's own named prohibition and the samekh at 6:15 both converge on a real seam one full sub-unit later. A full merge of 6:10-19, as one challenge proposed, is also defensible in that 6:13 alone cannot bear the weight of a boundary, but it overlooks the Masoretic section break that does exist at 6:15, one verse earlier than this span's new opening.

boundary_rationale: A scripted father-son catechesis opens on its own question formula, “When your son asks you in time to come, saying, What do the testimonies…mean?” (כִּי יִשְׁאָלְךָ בִנְךָ מָחָר לֵאמֹר), closing ch.6 on the “it shall be righteousness to us” formula before ch.7’s conquest-law address opens fresh.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A reviewer could split the question (v.20) from the scripted answer (vv.21-25), but the answer is explicitly framed as direct speech Moses supplies for the parent to give (“then you shall tell your son”), one continuous scripted exchange rather than two independent units.

boundary_rationale: Ch.7 opens the conquest-law address proper on its own conditional, “When Yahweh your God brings you into the land…and casts out many nations before you” (כִּי יְבִיאֲךָ יְהוָה אֱלֹהֶיךָ אֶל הָאָרֶץ…וְנָשַׁל גּוֹיִם רַבִּים מִפָּנֶיךָ), naming the seven nations and the herem, no-covenant, no-intermarriage rules, closing on the holy-people rationale before a shift to election theology opens v.7.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A reviewer could keep vv.1-11 as one election-and-herem unit, but v.7’s “Yahweh didn’t set his love on you…because you were more in number” pivots from concrete prohibitions to abstract theological argument about the ground of election, a real shift in mode.

boundary_rationale: The argument turns explicitly abstract at v.7, 'Yahweh didn't set his love on you nor choose you, because you were more in number...but because Yahweh loves you' (לֹ֣א מֵֽרֻבְּכֶ֞ם...כִּ֚י מֵֽאַהֲבַ֤ת יְהוָה֙ אֶתְכֶ֔ם), grounding obedience in love and oath rather than merit. The verse echoes 7:6's closing verb (בָּחַר, 'chose') but is its own main clause with its own subject and predicate, a rhetorical hinge picking up a word, not a grammatical continuation of the prior sentence. Both edges of this decision carry Masoretic support: a samekh closes 7:6 immediately before this span begins, and a petuchah — the heaviest class of division Torah paragraphing offers — closes 7:11 exactly at the span's end, closing on the 'keep the covenant' formula before the blessing catalog opens v.12.
strongest_rejected_alternative: The root repetition invites reading v.7 as a clarification hanging directly off v.6's election claim, in which case 045 and 046 should merge into one span, Deut.7.1-7.11. I decline: v.7 has its own finite verbs and its own subject, launching a fresh not-X-but-Y argument in a different rhetorical register from the concrete herem instructions of vv.1-6, and the petuchah at 7:11 independently confirms that MT itself treats the material ending there as a closed section, distinct from the case-law list before it.

The unit closes ch.9 on the covenant-inheritance appeal, corroborated by a petuchah landing exactly at the end of v.29.
strongest_rejected_alternative: One might read vv.15-29 as one continuous intercession scene with no internal seam, since the posture-and-prayer material is thematically unbroken; I decline because v.25's resumptive וָאֶתְנַפַּל and its matching forty-day phrase deliberately echo v.18 to mark a fresh telling — the narrative circles back to re-narrate the prostration before quoting the prayer that accompanied it, a real structural restart even without a change in grammatical person.

boundary_rationale: The climactic summary exhortation opens on its own rhetorical question, 'Now, Israel, what does Yahweh your God require of you' (וְעַתָּה֙ יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל מָ֚ה יְהוָ֣ה אֱלֹהֶ֔יךָ שֹׁאֵ֖ל מֵעִמָּ֑ךְ כִּ֣י אִם לְ֠יִרְאָה אֶת יְהוָ֨ה אֱלֹהֶ֜יךָ לָלֶ֤כֶת בְּכָל דְּרָכָיו֙ וּלְאַהֲבָ֣ה אֹת֔וֹ וְלַֽעֲבֹד֙ אֶת יְהוָ֣ה אֱלֹהֶ֔יךָ בְּכָל לְבָבְךָ֖ וּבְכָל נַפְשֶֽׁךָ), following directly on the petuchah at 10:11, and moves through God's supremacy, impartial justice, and love for the foreigner to a closing infinitive series in 10:12-13 (לִשְׁמֹ֞ר אֶת מִצְוֺ֤ת יְהוָה֙ וְאֶת חֻקֹּתָ֔יו אֲשֶׁ֛ר אָנֹכִ֥י מְצַוְּךָ֖ הַיּ֑וֹם לְט֖וֹב לָֽךְ) that 11:1's weqatal pair directly resumes: 'You shall love Yahweh your God, and keep his instructions' (וְאָ֣הַבְתָּ֔ אֵ֖ת יְהוָ֣ה אֱלֹהֶ֑יךָ וְשָׁמַרְתָּ֣ מִשְׁמַרְתּ֗וֹ וְחֻקֹּתָ֧יו וּמִשְׁפָּטָ֛יו וּמִצְוֺתָ֖יו כָּל הַיָּמִֽים) is the finite verb answering the infinitives just given, not a fresh address. The span now closes at 11:1, immediately before 11:2 opens a plural retrospective recital, 'you have known this day... your eyes have seen' (וִֽידַעְתֶּם֮ הַיּוֹם֒ ... ; כִּ֤י עֵֽינֵיכֶם֙ הָֽרֹאֹ֔ת אֶת כָּל מַעֲשֵׂ֥ה יְהוָ֖ה הַגָּדֹ֑ל אֲשֶׁ֖ר עָשָֽׂה) -- a shift in content, from second-singular exhortation to a plural generation-facing recital of the wilderness deeds, not the plural marking by itself. Person and number shift on their own do not discriminate this seam from two others inside the very span this decision draws: 10:15 is singular (רַ֧ק בַּאֲבֹתֶ֛יךָ חָשַׁ֥ק יְהוָ֖ה לְאַהֲבָ֣ה אוֹתָ֑ם וַיִּבְחַ֞ר בְּזַרְעָ֣ם אַחֲרֵיהֶ֗ם בָּכֶ֛ם מִכָּל הָעַמִּ֖ים כַּיּ֥וֹם הַזֶּה) and 10:16 turns plural (וּמַלְתֶּ֕ם אֵ֖ת עָרְלַ֣ת לְבַבְכֶ֑ם וְעָ֨רְפְּכֶ֔ם לֹ֥א תַקְשׁ֖וּ עֽוֹד), and 10:19 is plural (וַאֲהַבְתֶּ֖ם אֶת הַגֵּ֑ר כִּֽי גֵרִ֥ים הֱיִיתֶ֖ם בְּאֶ֥רֶץ מִצְרָֽיִם) while 10:20 returns to singular (אֶת יְהוָ֧ה אֱלֹהֶ֛יךָ תִּירָ֖א אֹת֣וֹ תַעֲבֹ֑ד וּב֣וֹ תִדְבָּ֔ק וּבִשְׁמ֖וֹ תִּשָּׁבֵֽעַ), and neither internal alternation is treated as a seam. What distinguishes 11:1|11:2 from those two is that the shift there coincides with a change of discourse mode -- exhortation giving way to retrospective recital addressed to a new audience horizon ('not your children, who have not known and have not seen') -- while the internal shifts at 10:15|16 and 10:19|20 are register variation within one continuous exhortation, not a change of what is being done with the discourse. No Masoretic mark falls anywhere inside this stretch -- the petuchah at 10:11 and the samekh at 11:9 bracket the whole of 10:12-11:9 without an internal break -- so this internal close rests on the content-and-discourse-mode turn, honestly disclosed as unmarked and as co-occurring with, but not reducible to, a person shift that recurs elsewhere in the span without effect.
strongest_rejected_alternative: The chapter line at 10:22|11:1 offers a tempting stopping point, and the earlier draft asserted a new address opens there; checked against the Hebrew, nothing supports it -- 11:1 is second-singular throughout, continuing 10:12-13's own infinitive series rather than opening independent content, and the real new movement doesn't arrive until 11:2's plural retrospective recital, וִידַעְתֶּם; that number shift co-occurs with the discourse-mode turn to recital rather than causing it, since the same kind of shift recurs unremarked at 10:15|16 and 10:19|20 without marking anything. The chapter number was doing work the grammar does not.

oshb:Deut.11.7 כִּ֤י עֵֽינֵיכֶם֙ הָֽרֹאֹ֔ת אֶת כָּל מַעֲשֵׂ֥ה יְהוָ֖ה הַגָּדֹ֑ל אֲשֶׁ֖ר עָשָֽׂה (retrospective recital continues in v.2's mode)
parashah_two_witness: petuchah after Deut.10.11 (opens this span); samekh after Deut.11.9; nothing marked between

boundary_rationale: The retrospective proper opens on a plural verb marking a real address shift, 'And you shall know today...that it was not your children (who have not known...)' (וִֽידַעְתֶּם֮ הַיּוֹם֒ כִּ֣י לֹ֣א אֶת בְּנֵיכֶ֗ם), switching from 11:1's second-singular continuation of 10:12-13's infinitive series into second-plural address that holds through the Exodus-wonders catalogue and the Dathan-and-Abiram episode, closing on 'your eyes have seen' (v.7) before a fresh imperative to keep the entire commandment opens v.8. No Masoretic mark exists at the 11:1|11:2 join itself; the petuchah after 10:11 and the samekh after 11:9 bracket this whole stretch without an internal break, so the boundary rests on the person-and-number shift alone.
strongest_rejected_alternative: One could keep 11:1 as this unit's opener, reading the whole of 10:12-11:7 as one address; I decline because 11:1's verbs remain second-singular, directly continuing 10:12-13's own infinitive series (an antecedent 11:1's finite verb resumes rather than a fresh command), while the retrospective's own plural marker, וִידַעְתֶּם, does not arrive until v.2 — the true address shift, and the more defensible opening edge.
boundary_evidence_refs: oshb:Deut.11.2 וִֽידַעְתֶּם֮ הַיּוֹם֒ כִּ֣י לֹ֣א אֶת בְּנֵיכֶ֗ם אֲשֶׁ֤ר לֹֽא יָדְעוּ֙
oshb:Deut.11.1 וְאָ֣הַבְתָּ֔ אֵ֖ת יְהוָ֣ה אֱלֹהֶ֑יךָ וְשָׁמַרְתָּ֣ מִשְׁמַרְתּ֗וֹ
oshb:Deut.11.7 כִּ֣י עֵינֵיכֶ֗ם הָרֹאֹת֙
parashah_two_witness: petuchah after Deut.10.11; samekh after Deut.11.9; nothing marked at the 11.1/11.2 join

boundary_rationale: A fresh imperative opens the unit, “Therefore you shall keep the entire commandment which I command you today” (וּשְׁמַרְתֶּם אֶת כָּל הַמִּצְוָה), contrasting Canaan’s rain-watered land with Egypt’s foot-irrigated fields, closing on “from the beginning of the year even to the end of the year” before the conditional rain-blessing formula opens v.13.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This land-contrast could be merged with the conditional rain promise that follows as one agricultural argument; instead, v.13’s “It shall happen, if you shall listen diligently” opens a fresh formal conditional (protasis-apodosis) distinct from the descriptive contrast that precedes it.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Deut.11.10 “For the land, where you go in to possess isn’t like the land of Egypt that you came out of…
oshb:Deut.11.12 עֵינֵי יְהוָה אֱלֹהֶיךָ בָּהּ מֵרֵשִׁית הַשָּׁנָה וְעַד אַחֲרִית שָׁנָה

boundary_rationale: A formal conditional opens the unit, “It shall happen, if you shall listen diligently to my commandments…that I will give the rain for your land in its season” (וְהָיָה אִם שָׁמֹעַ תִּשְׁמְעוּ אֶל מִצְוֺתַי…וְנָתַתִּי מְטַר אַרְצְכֶם בְּעִתּוֹ), pairing the positive rain-blessing with its negative mirror (shut heavens, perish quickly), closing before the household-transmission refrain reopens v.18.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A reviewer might read this as inseparable from vv.18-21 since both echo ch.6’s Shema household instructions, but v.18’s “Therefore you shall lay up these words” opens the same distinct transmission-instruction genre used at 6:6-9, formally separate from this conditional’s blessing-and-curse structure.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Deut.11.14 “that I will give the rain for your land in its season, the early rain and the latter rain…
oshb:Deut.11.17 וַאֲבַדְתֶּם מְהֵרָה מֵעַל הָאָרֶץ הַטֹּבָה אֲשֶׁר יְהוָה נֹתֵן לָכֶם

boundary_rationale: The transmission-instruction refrain recurs almost verbatim from 6:6-9, “You shall lay up these words of mine in your heart…bind them for a sign on your hand” (וְשַׂמְתֶּם אֶת דְּבָרַי אֵלֶּה עַל לְבַבְכֶם…וּקְשַׁרְתֶּם אֹתָם לְאוֹת עַל יֶדְכֶם), closing on the prolonged-days-like-the-heavens formula before a fresh diligent-keeping conditional opens v.22.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A reviewer could treat this refrain as inseparable from the surrounding rain conditional as one continuous exhortation, but its close verbal match to the distinct 6:6-9 unit shows it functions as the book’s own recurring formula, deserving the same boundary treatment given there.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Deut.11.18 “Therefore you shall lay up these words of mine in your heart and in your soul…
oshb:Deut.11.21 לְמַעַן יִרְבּוּ יְמֵיכֶם וִימֵי בְנֵיכֶם עַל הָאֲדָמָה

boundary_rationale: A fresh diligent-keeping conditional opens on “For if you shall diligently keep all these commandments…then Yahweh will drive out all these nations” (כִּי אִם שָׁמֹר תִּשְׁמְרוּן אֶת כָּל הַמִּצְוָה הַזֹּאת…וְהוֹרִישׁ יְהוָה), promising total dispossession and universal dread, closing before the blessing-and-curse formula opens v.26.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Merging this with the closing blessing-and-curse unit as one continuous promise is defensible on paper, yet v.26’s “Behold, I set before you today a blessing and a curse” opens a fresh, formally distinct declaration (a binary choice formula) rather than continuing the total-dispossession promise’s own logic.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Deut.11.23 “then Yahweh will drive out all these nations from before you, and you shall dispossess nations greater and mightier than yourselves.
oshb:Deut.11.25 פַּחְדְּכֶם וּמוֹרַאֲכֶם יִתֵּן יְהוָה אֱלֹהֵיכֶם עַל פְּנֵי כָל הָאָרֶץ

boundary_rationale: The binary-choice formula opens the unit, 'Behold, I set before you today a blessing and a curse' (רְאֵ֗ה אָנֹכִ֛י נֹתֵ֥ן לִפְנֵיכֶ֖ם הַיּ֑וֹם בְּרָכָ֖ה וּקְלָלָֽה), stating the terms of blessing (obedience) and curse (turning aside after other gods) in vv.27-28, and closing on a setumah that falls at the end of 11:28 — corroboration the original span never engaged. Splitting the deposition of that blessing and curse onto specific mountains (vv.29-32) into its own decision honors both the Masoretic section mark and the fresh protasis that opens it (see the new sibling decision).
strongest_rejected_alternative: The whole of 11:26-32 reads smoothly as one instruction — declare the choice, then say where to enact it — and could be kept merged on that thematic continuity alone, which is what the original entry did. I now reject that reading because a setumah, not merely its absence, sits at the exact seam being crossed, and 11:29's opening formula matches a pattern this campaign already credits as unit-opening elsewhere in the same chapter; treating the formula one way at 11:13 and another way here was the inconsistency the challenge correctly named.

oshb:Deut.11.28 וְהַקְּלָלָ֗ה אִם לֹ֤א תִשְׁמְעוּ֙ אֶל מִצְוֺת֙ יְהוָ֣ה אֱלֹֽהֵיכֶ֔ם
oshb:Deut.11.13 וְהָיָ֗ה אִם שָׁמֹ֤עַ תִּשְׁמְעוּ֙
parashah_two_witness: samekh after Deut.11.28

boundary_rationale: A fresh protasis opens the unit, 'It shall be, when Yahweh your God brings you into the land that you are going in to possess it' (וְהָיָ֗ה כִּ֤י יְבִֽיאֲךָ֙ יְהוָ֣ה אֱלֹהֶ֔יךָ אֶל הָאָ֕רֶץ), the same וְהָיָה כִּי/אִם formula this campaign already treats as unit-opening at 11:13, here directing where the blessing and curse just declared (11:26-28) are to be deposited — on Gerizim and Ebal — before a closing geographic aside and the charge to observe all the statutes that bridges into the law code's own heading at 12:1. A setumah closes 11:28 immediately before this span begins, corroborating the split from the preceding decision.
strongest_rejected_alternative: One could read this material as inseparable from the blessing-curse declaration it enacts, one continuous instruction from proclamation to deposition; I split it instead because the setumah after 11:28 marks a real Masoretic division at exactly this seam, and the fresh וְהָיָה כִּי protasis matches a construction this campaign elsewhere credits as unit-opening, so treating it as subordinate here alone would be an inconsistent application of the same rule.
boundary_evidence_refs: oshb:Deut.11.29 וְהָיָ֗ה כִּ֤י יְבִֽיאֲךָ֙ יְהוָ֣ה אֱלֹהֶ֔יךָ אֶל הָאָ֕רֶץ אֲשֶׁר אַתָּ֥ה בָא שָׁ֖מָּה לְרִשְׁתָּ֑הּ וְנָתַתָּ֤ה אֶת הַבְּרָכָה֙ עַל הַ֣ר גְּרִזִ֔ים וְאֶת הַקְּלָלָ֖ה עַל הַ֥ר עֵיבָֽל
oshb:Deut.11.32 וּשְׁמַרְתֶּ֣ם לַעֲשׂ֔וֹת אֵ֥ת כָּל הַֽחֻקִּ֖ים וְאֶת הַמִּשְׁפָּטִ֑ים
parashah_two_witness: samekh after Deut.11.28 (opens this span, by closing the preceding decision)

boundary_rationale: The law code proper opens on its own אֵלֶּה-colophon, “These are the statutes and the ordinances which you shall observe to do in the land” (אֵלֶּה הַחֻקִּים וְהַמִּשְׁפָּטִים אֲשֶׁר תִּשְׁמְרוּן לַעֲשׂוֹת בָּאָרֶץ), matching the same heading device used at 1:1 and 4:44 to mark a fresh major section, distinct from the centralization instructions themselves that open v.2.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A reviewer might fold this heading directly into the centralization law that follows as its opening clause, but the campaign’s own weighting treats an אֵלֶּה-colophon as a strong boundary marker in its own right, generalizing what follows into a standing heading rather than beginning the first case itself.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Deut.12.1 “These are the statutes and the ordinances which you shall observe to do in the land which Yahweh, the God of your fathers, has given you to possess…
oshb:Deut.12.1 אֵלֶּה הַחֻקִּים וְהַמִּשְׁפָּטִים אֲשֶׁר תִּשְׁמְרוּן לַעֲשׂוֹת בָּאָרֶץ

boundary_rationale: The first case opens on its own imperative, “You shall surely destroy all the places in which the nations…served their gods” (אַבֵּד תְּאַבְּדוּן אֶת כָּל הַמְּקֹמוֹת), pivoting to the positive centralization command (“to the place which Yahweh your God shall choose”), closing on the eat-and-rejoice formula before the “not as we do here today” contrast opens v.8.
strongest_rejected_alternative: The destroy-pagan-sites command (vv.2-3) and the choose-the-place command (vv.4-7) could be split into two decisions, but v.4’s “You shall not do so to Yahweh your God” is the direct antithetical pivot answering vv.2-3, one continuous contrast rather than two independent cases.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Deut.12.2 “You shall surely destroy all the places in which the nations that you shall dispossess served their gods…
oshb:Deut.12.7 וַאֲכַלְתֶּם שָׁם לִפְנֵי יְהוָה אֱלֹהֵיכֶם וּשְׂמַחְתֶּם בְּכֹל מִשְׁלַח יֶדְכֶם

boundary_rationale: A fresh contrast opens on “You shall not do all the things that we do here today, every man whatever is right in his own eyes” (לֹא תַעֲשׂוּן כְּכֹל אֲשֶׁר אֲנַחְנוּ עֹשִׂים פֹּה הַיּוֹם), projecting the future settled, centralized worship, closing on the household-and-Levite rejoicing formula before the sacrifice-location prohibition opens v.13.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This present/future contrast could be treated as continuous with the preceding destroy-and-choose command, one undivided centralization argument; even so, its own fresh negative formula (“You shall not do…as we do here today”) opens a distinct rhetorical contrast (wilderness improvisation versus settled order) not present in vv.2-7.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Deut.12.8 “You shall not do all the things that we do here today, every man whatever is right in his own eyes;
oshb:Deut.12.12 וְהַלֵּוִי אֲשֶׁר בְּשַׁעֲרֵיכֶם כִּי אֵין לוֹ חֵלֶק וְנַחֲלָה אִתְּכֶם

boundary_rationale: A fresh case-law formula opens on “Be careful that you don’t offer your burnt offerings in every place that you see” (הִשָּׁמֶר לְךָ פֶּן תַּעֲלֶה עֹלֹתֶיךָ בְּכָל מָקוֹם אֲשֶׁר תִּרְאֶה), permitting profane slaughter for ordinary meat at home while restricting offerings to the chosen place, closing on the do-not-forsake-the-Levite refrain before the expanded meat-eating case opens v.20.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the sacrifice-location prohibition (vv.13-14) from the profane-slaughter permission (vv.15-19) is one option, but v.15’s “Yet you may kill and eat meat” is explicitly framed as a concession answering the very restriction just stated, one continuous ruling.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Deut.12.13 “Be careful that you don’t offer your burnt offerings in every place that you see;
oshb:Deut.12.19 הִשָּׁמֶר לְךָ פֶּן תַּעֲזֹב אֶת הַלֵּוִי כָּל יָמֶיךָ עַל אַדְמָתֶךָ

boundary_rationale: A fresh conditional opens the expanded case, “When Yahweh your God enlarges your border, as he has promised you, and you say, I want to eat meat” (כִּי יַרְחִיב יְהוָה אֱלֹהֶיךָ אֶת גְּבוּלְךָ…וְאָמַרְתָּ אֹכְלָה בָשָׂר), restating the blood prohibition and the holy-things rule, closing on the “do what is good and right” formula before the warning against inquiring after pagan practices opens v.29.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A reviewer might treat vv.20-28 as inseparable from vv.13-19 since both regulate meat-eating, but v.20’s own fresh conditional (border enlargement enabling greater distance from the sanctuary) marks a distinct triggering scenario rather than restating the prior ruling.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Deut.12.20 “When Yahweh your God enlarges your border, as he has promised you, and you say, ‘I want to eat meat,’…
oshb:Deut.12.28 שְׁמֹר וְשָׁמַעְתָּ אֵת כָּל הַדְּבָרִים הָאֵלֶּה אֲשֶׁר אָנֹכִי מְצַוֶּךָּ

boundary_rationale: A fresh warning opens on 'When Yahweh your God cuts off the nations...be careful that you...not inquire after their gods' (כִּֽי יַכְרִית֩ יְהוָ֨ה אֱלֹהֶ֜יךָ אֶת הַגּוֹיִ֗ם...הִשָּׁ֣מֶר לְךָ֔ פֶּן תִּנָּקֵ֖שׁ), closing the centralization laws on the canon formula, WEB 12:32 = MT 13:1: 'this word which I command you, that you shall observe to do — you shall not add to it, nor take away from it' (אֵ֣ת כָּל הַדָּבָ֗ר אֲשֶׁ֤ר אָנֹכִי֙ מְצַוֶּ֣ה אֶתְכֶ֔ם אֹת֥וֹ תִשְׁמְר֖וּ לַעֲשׂ֑וֹת לֹא תֹסֵ֣ף עָלָ֔יו וְלֹ֥א תִגְרַ֖ע מִמֶּֽנּוּ). A petuchah — the strongest class of Masoretic division — sits at the end of this verse (MT 13:1), with nothing marked anywhere between the setumah closing 12:28 and that petuchah, so the manuscript tradition delimits exactly this stretch, MT 12:29-13:1, as one closed section. The שְׁמֹר...אֵת כָּל...אֲשֶׁ֥ר אָנֹכִ֖י מְצַוֶּ֑ךָּ frame that closes 12:28 recurs almost verbatim to close 13:1 — a doubled closing device, not an opening one — and הַדָּבָר's definiteness here is grammatically identical to its use at 4:2 (לֹ֣א תֹסִ֗פוּ עַל הַדָּבָר֙ אֲשֶׁ֤ר אָנֹכִי֙ מְצַוֶּ֣ה אֶתְכֶ֔ם), where the reference is unmistakably forward (cataphoric) rather than backward: the noun is made definite by its own relative clause in both places, not by pointing at what precedes. The one real counter-signal is a Numeruswechsel across the seam — 12:28-31 stays second-singular throughout (הִשָּׁמֶר לְךָ, תִּנָּקֵשׁ, תִּדְרֹשׁ, תַּעֲשֶׂה), MT 13:1 opens plural (אֶתְכֶם, תִשְׁמְרוּ) and closes singular (תֹסֵף, תִגְרַע), and MT 13:2 is singular again — logged here as live evidence, weighed against, and outweighed by, the petuchah and the doubled closing frame. Confidence moves from low to medium on the strength of this corrected and better-corroborated ground.
strongest_rejected_alternative: The chapter division itself, and MT's own placement of 13:1 as the first verse of ch.13, invite reading the canon formula as the false-prophet law's own opening line rather than the centralization law's close. Checked directly, that reading requires the article on הַדָּבָר to point backward to the legislative complex just given; the identical construction at 4:2 shows the same definite-by-relative-clause pattern pointing forward instead, which removes that reading's main textual support. The Numeruswechsel is the one piece of evidence still favoring a fresh opening at MT 13:1 or 13:2, and it is disclosed rather than dismissed, but it stands alone against a petuchah and a repeated closing formula.

boundary_rationale: Verse 21 closes the dietary code with two prohibitions that share no vocabulary: the carrion clause, governing a self-dead animal (נְבֵלָה) that may be given to the foreigner within one's gates or sold to a foreigner, and the kid-in-milk clause, which opens its own fresh לֹא + verb with no term in common with the first -- לֹֽא תְבַשֵּׁ֥ל גְּדִ֖י בַּחֲלֵ֥ב אִמּֽוֹ, 'you shall not boil a kid in its mother's milk.' That lexical break is real, but it falls within a single verse with no intervening verse number, so it does not itself force a split, and it is not evidence for either edge of this decision. The closing edge is well made: a petuchah -- the strongest divider the two-witness apparatus carries -- stands after 14:21 itself, closing the whole clean-food code before v.22 opens the tithe law on its own topic (עַשֵּׂ֣ר תְּעַשֵּׂ֔ר, 'you shall surely tithe'). The opening edge at 14:20|21 needs its own ground, since no pe or samekh site exists at Deut.14.20 in the two-witness file and a mark at the far edge cannot supply evidence for the near one under mesh-r2, where markers corroborate rather than drive. That ground is a polarity flip on the same root: 14:20 grants permission with a positive verb, כָּל ע֥וֹף טָה֖וֹר תֹּאכֵֽלוּ ('every clean bird you may eat'), and 14:21 reverses polarity on the same root, לֹ֣א תֹאכְל֣וּ כָל נְ֠בֵלָה ('you shall not eat any carrion'), while also leaving the winged-creature taxonomy of vv.11-20 for carrion of any kind. With the opening edge carrying a genuine text signal but no marker at all, and the closing edge carrying both marker and topic-turn, confidence is capped at medium rather than high.

boundary_rationale: The Asherah-pole and sacred-pillar prohibitions are bound by a plain waw-coordination and an identical negative-dative frame: לֹֽא תִטַּ֥ע לְךָ֛ אֲשֵׁרָ֖ה ('you shall not plant an Asherah for yourself') is answered directly by וְלֹֽא תָקִ֥ים לְךָ֖ מַצֵּבָ֑ה ('and you shall not set up a pillar for yourself'), the same לֹא + finite verb + לְךָ shape carried across the verse line by v.22's opening ו — a real syntactic bond, not merely a shared topic. Against that bond stands a setumah after v.21 itself, internal to this span, marking a genuine division point the Masoretic tradition offers between the two prohibitions; disclosed rather than suppressed, it is real countervailing evidence for treating them as two decisions instead of one.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A reviewer could split at the internal setumah after v.21, treating the Asherah-pole prohibition and the pillar prohibition as two separate one-verse decisions, matching the manuscript's own granularity there; I merge them instead because the waw-coordination and the matching לֹא...לְךָ frame bind v.22 to v.21 as one continuous unit rather than two independent commands. But the internal mark is real countervailing evidence, not merely absent, and confidence stays low to reflect that.

boundary_rationale: A single-verse prohibition, 'you shall not sacrifice to Yahweh your God an ox or a sheep in which is a defect' (לֹא תִזְבַּח֩ לַיהוָ֨ה אֱלֹהֶ֜יךָ שׁ֣וֹר וָשֶׂ֗ה אֲשֶׁ֨ר יִהְיֶ֥ה בוֹ֙ מ֔וּם...), stands bracketed by a setumah on each side -- one after 16:22 closing the Asherah-pole/pillar pair, another after 17:1 itself -- both of the same samekh class that also stands after 16:20 and, internal to the preceding decision (096), after 16:21. The object class shifts across that first bracket, from planted or erected cultic objects (אֲשֵׁרָה, מַצֵּבָה) to a sacrificial animal's physical qualification (שׁוֹר וָשֶׂה ... מוּם), a genuine content break rather than the chapter number, and the setumah bracket corroborates it on both ends before the idolatry-investigation case law opens its own fresh כִּי protasis at v.2. That bracket is corroboration only, not the driver, and it is not distinctive within its own neighborhood: 096, the immediately preceding decision, treats a setumah of this same class -- the one after 16:21 -- as real countervailing evidence it merges across rather than as confidence-lifting support, so the same marker class cannot be overridable at 16:21 and confidence-raising at 16:22/17:1 without an argument for the asymmetry, and none is available. The break across the 16:22|17:1 seam is also less clean than a bare object-class shift suggests: 16:22 closes on אֲשֶׁ֥ר שָׂנֵ֖א יְהוָ֥ה אֱלֹהֶֽיךָ ('which Yahweh your God hates') and 17:1 closes on כִּ֧י תוֹעֲבַ֛ת יְהוָ֥ה אֱלֹהֶ֖יךָ הֽוּא ('for it is an abomination to Yahweh your God') -- both prohibitions end on the same kind of divine-attitude rationale clause, a formal tie running across the very seam this decision calls a clean content break. Disclosed rather than suppressed, that residual link, together with the marker-class asymmetry against 096, caps confidence at medium: the object-class shift and the setumah bracket still support the span, but neither the marker class nor the content break is as clean as a high rating would require.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A reviewer could keep this bound to 16:21-22 as one three-verse altar-purity unit, since all three verses concern cultic objects and offerings broadly; I treat 17:1 as its own case instead because the setumah after 16:22 already closes the pole/pillar pair on manuscript grounds, and the object class changes cleanly at 17:1 — a planted pole or erected pillar becomes a sacrificial animal's bodily defect — with a second setumah closing 17:1 itself before the idolatry case opens at v.2.

boundary_rationale: A temporal clause opens on 'It shall be, when he sits on the throne of his kingdom, that he shall write himself a copy of this law' (וְהָיָ֣ה כְשִׁבְתּ֔וֹ עַ֖ל כִּסֵּ֣א מַמְלַכְתּ֑וֹ וְכָ֨תַב ל֜וֹ אֶת מִשְׁנֵ֨ה הַתּוֹרָ֤ה הַזֹּאת֙ עַל סֵ֔פֶר מִלִּפְנֵ֥י הַכֹּהֲנִ֖ים הַלְוִיִּֽם), closing ch.17 and the king law on the not-lifted-up-above-his-brothers formula. This decision is held at low confidence rather than lifted from insufficient_evidence: WLC brackets the whole of 17:14-20 as one paragraph, with no mark internal to it; the sole textual argument for the cut, the וְהָיָה כְשִׁבְתּוֹ clause, has no Masoretic corroboration of its own; and the same formula-family (וְהָיָה כִּי/אִם/כְ) receives inconsistent treatment across this book -- unit-opening at 11:13 where a setumah backs it, contested as unit-opening at 11:29 within this same range, and now asserted here with no marker at all. The grammatical-subject claim once made for this span is corrected rather than repeated: the whole of vv.15-20 is not uniformly third-person. 17:15 addresses the people directly in the second singular about installing the king (שׂ֣וֹם תָּשִׂ֤ים עָלֶ֨יךָ֙ מֶ֔לֶךְ אֲשֶׁ֥ר יִבְחַ֛ר יְהוָ֥ה אֱלֹהֶ֖יךָ בּ֑וֹ מִקֶּ֣רֶב אַחֶ֗יךָ תָּשִׂ֤ים עָלֶ֨יךָ֙ מֶ֔לֶךְ לֹ֣א תוּכַ֗ל לָתֵ֤ת עָלֶ֨יךָ֙ אִ֣ישׁ נָכְרִ֔י אֲשֶׁ֥ר לֹֽא אָחִ֖יךָ הֽוּא), and 17:16 turns to the people again in the plural mid-verse, citing Yahweh's own prior word to them (וַֽיהוָה֙ אָמַ֣ר לָכֶ֔ם לֹ֣א תֹסִפ֗וּן, 'you shall never again return that way'). Because that plural citation still falls inside v.16, the uninterrupted third-person-singular run about the king cannot begin at 17:16b as earlier stated; it begins only at 17:17 (וְלֹ֤א יַרְבֶּה לּוֹ֙ נָשִׁ֔ים וְלֹ֥א יָס֖וּר לְבָב֑וֹ וְכֶ֣סֶף וְזָהָ֔ב לֹ֥א יַרְבֶּה לּ֖וֹ מְאֹֽד), the first verse entirely after the plural re-addressing, and continues without a further re-addressing of the people through v.20. That narrower run is what argues, weakly, for treating v.18 as a fresh moment within it, and this held-low disposition is unchanged by the correction.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Reading 17:14-20 as one undivided king law, closed only by the setumah after v.20, is at least as defensible as the split: nothing marks the 17|18 seam internally, the subject does not shift again after 17:16, and the accumulation clauses of vv.16-17 and the writing clause of v.18 are equally third-person predications about the same figure. I do not adopt the merge outright because the temporal clause at v.18 does mark a real shift in the king's own timeline (a later moment, once enthroned, rather than the initial restrictions on his power), but I also do not force the split to a confident verdict, since neither reading has the kind of textual or Masoretic support this campaign otherwise requires.

boundary_rationale: Ch.18 opens on Levi's landless-status principle, 'The priests and the Levites — all the tribe of Levi — shall have no portion nor inheritance with Israel' (לֹֽא יִ֠הְיֶה לַכֹּהֲנִ֨ים הַלְוִיִּ֜ם כָּל שֵׁ֧בֶט לֵוִ֛י חֵ֥לֶק וְנַחֲלָ֖ה עִם יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל), closing on the same principle restated in v.2 ('Yahweh is his inheritance'), before a fresh schedule-head formula opens the specific priestly dues in v.3 (see the new sibling decision). A setumah closes v.2 exactly at this span's end, corroborating the split.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Keeping vv.1-5 merged as one continuous priestly-support unit reads smoothly, since the dues in vv.3-5 illustrate the principle just stated; the setumah after v.2 and the formula-headed opening of v.3 — the same וְזֶה + construct-noun device used at 15:2 and 19:4 to open a schedule — both mark a real internal seam the merged reading would erase.

boundary_rationale: A fresh schedule-head formula opens the unit, 'And this shall be the priests' due from the people' (וְזֶ֡ה יִהְיֶה֩ מִשְׁפַּ֨ט הַכֹּהֲנִ֜ים מֵאֵ֣ת הָעָ֗ם), the same וְזֶה + construct-noun device this campaign already credits as opening a schedule at 15:2 (וְזֶה֮ דְּבַ֣ר הַשְּׁמִטָּה֒) and 19:4 (וְזֶה֙ דְּבַ֣ר הָרֹצֵ֔חַ), listing the shoulder, jaws, and stomach from slaughtered animals, the firstfruits of grain, wine, oil, and fleece, closing on the election-and-service rationale (v.5) before the migrating-Levite case opens fresh at v.6. A setumah closes 18:2 immediately before this span begins, corroborating the split from the preceding decision.
strongest_rejected_alternative: The whole of 18:1-5 could remain one Levitical-support unit, general principle plus specific dues; the setumah after 18:2 and the formula-headed opening at v.3, matching a device this campaign treats as boundary-marking elsewhere in the same law code, both argue for treating the schedule as its own decision.

boundary_rationale: A fresh conditional opens the divination prohibition, 'When you have come into the land which Yahweh your God gives you, you shall not learn to imitate the abominations of those nations' (כִּ֤י אַתָּה֙ בָּ֣א אֶל הָאָ֔רֶץ...לֹֽא תִלְמַ֣ד לַעֲשׂ֔וֹת כְּתוֹעֲבֹ֖ת הַגּוֹיִ֥ם הָהֵֽם), cataloguing diviners, sorcerers, and necromancers, and closing on the self-sufficiency demand 'You shall be blameless before Yahweh your God' (תָּמִ֣ים תִּֽהְיֶ֔ה עִ֖ם יְהוָ֥ה אֱלֹהֶֽיךָ, v.13). A setumah closes v.13 exactly at this span's end; v.14's own contrastive clause, 'but Yahweh your God has not given you thus' (וְאַתָּ֕ה לֹ֣א כֵ֔ן נָ֛תַן לְךָ֖ יְהוָ֥ה אֱלֹהֶֽיךָ), is syntactically incomplete without v.15's answer and belongs to the following decision as its contrastive setup.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Keeping v.14 inside this decision, as originally drafted, reads the driven-out-because-of-abominations theme as running through the verse; that clause actually stands at v.12, one verse earlier, and v.14's own contrastive complement is left dangling without v.15 — the setumah after v.13 marks the more defensible close.

boundary_rationale: The contrastive setup opens on 'But Yahweh your God has not given you thus' (וְאַתָּ֕ה לֹ֣א כֵ֔ן נָ֛תַן לְךָ֖ יְהוָ֥ה אֱלֹהֶֽיךָ), the pivot of a them/you opposition that v.14 states and v.15 answers: the nations 'listen' to diviners and soothsayers (אֶל מְעֹנְנִ֥ים וְאֶל קֹסְמִ֖ים יִשְׁמָ֑עוּ) where Israel instead 'listens' to the prophet Yahweh raises up (אֵלָ֖יו תִּשְׁמָעֽוּן) -- the shared שמע root marking two different objects of the same verb of attention, deliberately set against each other rather than two independent statements. That contrast, not a syntactic dependency, is what binds v.14 to v.15: v.14's own clause is grammatically complete on its own (נָתַן takes the adverbial לֹא כֵן with לְךָ as its indirect object), and v.15 is an independent clause with its own verb (יָקִ֥ים), its own fronted object (נָבִ֨יא), and its own indirect object (לְךָ֖); v.15 supplies nothing that v.14's sentence itself lacks. The unit runs through Yahweh's ratifying speech (vv.17-19), grounded explicitly in the people's own Horeb request for a mediator (v.16), closing on the accountability formula before the false-prophet test opens with its own אַךְ pivot at v.20.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Opening this decision at v.15, as originally drafted, is defensible if v.14 is read purely as the divination law's closing generalization, complete in itself and not part of the mediator promise. Checked against the grammar, that reading is not ruled out syntactically -- v.14's clause does not depend on v.15 for its completion -- but it is ruled out by the them/you, שמע-root contrast the two verses build together, and the setumah closing v.13 (not v.14) confirms that the Masoretic tradition already treats v.14 as belonging with what follows rather than what precedes.

boundary_rationale: A single prohibition opens on 'You shall not sow your vineyard with two kinds of seed' (לֹא תִזְרַ֥ע כַּרְמְךָ֖ כִּלְאָ֑יִם), carrying its own elaborating פֶּן clause — lest the whole yield be forfeited — a structure the following pair does not share. It stands as its own case, bracketed by a setumah closing 22:8 before it and a setumah closing 22:9 at its own end, distinct in both vocabulary (כִּלְאָיִם, not the יַחְדָּו of what follows) and syntax from the paired ox-and-donkey and wool-and-linen prohibitions that come next.

A full three-way split, matching the individual setumah after each verse, is also defensible and arguably the more Masoretically faithful reading; I keep 10-11 merged rather than splitting them further because their wording and syntax genuinely match each other in a way v.9 does not match either (see the new sibling decision).

boundary_rationale: Two prohibitions share one exact closing formula and near-identical syntax: 'You shall not plow with an ox and a donkey together' (לֹֽא תַחֲרֹ֥שׁ בְּשׁוֹר וּבַחֲמֹ֖ר יַחְדָּֽו) and 'You shall not wear a mixed fabric, wool and linen together' (לֹ֤א תִלְבַּשׁ֙ שַֽׁעַטְנֵ֔ז צֶ֥מֶר וּפִשְׁתִּ֖ים יַחְדָּֽו), both closing on יַחְדָּו and both naming two disparate things joined that should stay apart — a genuine lexical and structural pairing that the seed-mixture prohibition immediately before them (22:9) does not share, since it lacks יַחְדָּו entirely and carries its own פֶּן clause instead. A setumah stands after each of 22:10 and 22:11 individually, marking against as well as for this merge; the shared formula is judged to outweigh the internal mark, but only at low confidence, since the Masoretic tradition itself keeps the two verses apart.
strongest_rejected_alternative: WLC's own individual setumah after 22:10 argues for keeping the two prohibitions apart as separate decisions, matching the manuscript's granularity exactly; I merge them instead because they are the only pair in this run of three that actually share both their closing word (יַחְדָּו) and their syntactic shape, a bond the seed-mixture prohibition preceding them lacks — but the internal mark is real countervailing evidence, not merely absent, and confidence is set low to reflect that.

boundary_rationale: A single-verse positive command, 'you shall make yourselves fringes on the four corners of your cloak' (גְּדִלִ֖ים תַּעֲשֶׂה לָּ֑ךְ עַל אַרְבַּ֛ע כַּנְפ֥וֹת כְּסוּתְךָ֖ אֲשֶׁ֥ר תְּכַסֶּה בָּֽהּ), stands as its own case between the mixture prohibitions and the virginity-dispute law: 22:9's לֹא תִזְרַ֥ע, 22:10's לֹֽא תַחֲרֹ֥שׁ and 22:11's לֹ֤א תִלְבַּשׁ֙ are all prohibitions, and 22:12 alone commands positively, before 22:13 opens a fresh case on its own כִּֽי יִקַּ֥ח protasis. That mood contrast -- the sole positive command in a run of לֹא-prohibitions -- is the text signal driving this decision. The setumah after 22:11 opening this span and the one after 22:12 closing it are real, but they are not distinctive within the run: Deut.22.9, 22.10, 22.11 and 22.12 each carry a samekh-class mark, so every member of the run is bracketed the same way, and the bracket around 22:12 corroborates the boundary without adding anything a plain content-and-mood reading does not already supply. That is the same configuration the campaign already prices at medium one verse earlier: M8-Deut-126 is a one-verse span in this identical series (22:9), bracketed by a samekh at each edge exactly as this one is, resting on a text signal of comparable weight -- a unique elaborating פֶּן clause and vocabulary distinct from its neighbors -- and it is priced medium. High for 127 and medium for 126 could not both stand without an explicit argument for treating 127's signal as stronger, and the mood contrast does not obviously outrank 126's grounds. Confidence is capped at medium so the two single-verse decisions in this run are priced alike.

boundary_rationale: The twelve-curse liturgy's shared ground is not primarily the offense named in each clause but the discrete performative response that closes it. This first curse, 'Cursed is the man who makes an engraved or molten image' -- oshb:Deut.27.15 אָר֣וּר הָאִ֡ישׁ אֲשֶׁ֣ר יַעֲשֶׂה֩ פֶ֨סֶל וּמַסֵּכָ֜ה תּוֹעֲבַ֣ת יְהוָ֗ה מַעֲשֵׂ֛ה יְדֵ֥י חָרָ֖שׁ וְשָׂ֣ם בַּסָּ֑תֶר וְעָנ֧וּ כָל הָעָ֛ם וְאָמְר֖וּ אָמֵֽן, is answered by the assembly's own plural variant of the series' refrain, וְעָנ֧וּ כָל הָעָ֛ם וְאָמְר֖וּ אָמֵֽן ('and all the people shall answer and say, Amen'); every one of the eleven curses that follow closes on the four-word singular form וְאָמַ֥ר כָּל הָעָ֖ם אָמֵֽן. That per-curse ritual response -- present without exception after all twelve entries -- is what the agricultural-futility catalog at 28:38-42 conspicuously lacks: five items sharing a fronted object, four of the five (vv.38-41) closed by a כִּי-clause naming the cause of loss and the fifth (v.42) fronting its object with no כִּי-clause at all, and none of the five closed by a response formula of any kind. Offense-differentiation among the twelve (idolatry here, filial dishonor next, and so on through incest, murder, and bribery) remains real color, but standing alone it is in tension with the 28:38-42 merge, which differentiates its own five items by object and agent just as clearly and is still read as one catalog. The performative-response criterion is what actually distinguishes a performed liturgy of twelve discrete units from an unbroken descriptive list. parashah_two_witness.json corroborates unusually densely here: a samekh follows every one of MT 27:15 through 27:25, and a petuchah -- the strongest class recorded anywhere in this book -- closes MT 27:26, an unbroken run of independent Masoretic section punctuation matching every one of the twelve seams. That density lifts confidence from low to medium.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Reading all twelve curses as one 27:15-26 register, on the model applied to the six-fold blessing/curse domain lists of ch.28, is the recurring objection; it is more evidence-full than it first appears, since ch.28's domain lists genuinely do lack any per-item response formula. Twelve seams that each close on their own Amen are formally closer to twelve performed cases than to one repeated-template blessing list, and the two-witness file's near-total marker density for this specific series (absent from the ch.28 blessing/curse registers) corroborates treating it differently.
boundary_evidence_refs: oshb:Deut.27.15 אָר֣וּר הָאִ֡ישׁ אֲשֶׁ֣ר יַעֲשֶׂה֩ פֶ֨סֶל וּמַסֵּכָ֜ה תּוֹעֲבַ֣ת יְהוָ֗ה מַעֲשֵׂ֛ה יְדֵ֥י חָרָ֖שׁ וְשָׂ֣ם בַּסָּ֑תֶר וְעָנ֧וּ כָל הָעָ֛ם וְאָמְר֖וּ אָמֵֽן (v.15 response variant: plural וְעָנוּ)
oshb:Deut.28.38 זֶ֥רַע רַ֖ב תּוֹצִ֣יא הַשָּׂדֶ֑ה וּמְעַ֣ט תֶּאֱסֹ֔ף כִּ֥י יַחְסְלֶ֖נּוּ הָאַרְבֶּֽה (כִּי-clause, no response formula)

parashah_two_witness: samekh after each of Deut.27.15 through Deut.27.25; petuchah after Deut.27.26 closes the series

boundary_rationale: The second curse turns from cultic to familial offense, 'Cursed is he who dishonors his father or his mother' -- oshb:Deut.27.16 אָרוּר מַקְלֶה אָבִיו וְאִמּוֹ, and closes on the series' standard singular response, וְאָמַר כָּל הָעָם אָמֵן. As established at M8-Deut-165, it is this discrete performative closure -- not the change of offense by itself -- that earns the curse its own decision; the fifth-commandment topic is color describing what the curse condemns, not the boundary evidence for where it ends.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Both this curse and the idolatry curse before it concern foundational covenant duties and could be read as one opening pair; each is instead bracketed by its own complete Amen response, a formally closed unit the liturgy performs individually rather than a continuous list punctuated only at its ends.
boundary_evidence_refs: oshb:Deut.27.16 אָרוּר מַקְלֶה אָבִיו וְאִמּוֹ וְאָמַר כָּל הָעָם אָמֵן
parashah_two_witness: samekh after Deut.27.16

boundary_rationale: Landmark-removal, the third curse, recasts the standalone statute of 19:14 into this liturgy's performed form: oshb:Deut.27.17 אָרוּר מַסִּיג גְּבוּל רֵעֵהוּ, closed by its own וְאָמַר כָּל הָעָם אָמֵן. The genre shift from case-law statute (19:14) to performed curse-with-response (here) is itself a text signal supporting independent treatment, on top of the discrete-closure criterion set out at M8-Deut-165.
strongest_rejected_alternative: The overlap with 19:14 might suggest this curse is a weaker candidate for independent status, being 'merely' a restatement; but its function here is liturgical performance answered by the assembly, not case law addressed to a judge, so it stands on the same footing as its eleven neighbors regardless of the doctrinal overlap.
boundary_evidence_refs: oshb:Deut.27.17 אָרוּר מַסִּיג גְּבוּל רֵעֵהוּ וְאָמַר כָּל הָעָם אָמֵן

boundary_rationale: Curse four turns to exploitation of the vulnerable, 'Cursed is he who leads the blind astray on the road' -- oshb:Deut.27.18 אָרוּר מַשְׁגֶּה עִוֵּר בַּדָּרֶךְ, closed by its own Amen. It sits adjacent to the justice-for-the-powerless curse that follows, sharing a broad theme with it, but each is a discrete performed unit under the criterion set out at M8-Deut-165, not a two-item block.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A reviewer might group this with the following curse against denying justice to the foreigner, fatherless, and widow as one 'protection of the weak' couplet; the liturgy's performance structure treats every entry alike regardless of thematic kinship, each closed by its own complete response.

boundary_rationale: The fifth entry names the code's recurring foreigner/fatherless/widow triad, echoing 24:17: oshb:Deut.27.19 אָרוּר מַטֶּה מִשְׁפַּט גֵּר יָתוֹם וְאַלְמָנָה, closed by its own Amen. That grouping is not adopted: the liturgy assigns each entry its own complete assembly response regardless of how closely its subject matter echoes a neighbor's, and a pairing built on theme rather than on the performed response would have to explain why none of the other eleven curses receive the same treatment, several of which share subject matter just as closely (the two neighbour-harm curses at vv.17 and 24, which share only the object רֵעֵהוּ and not the offence -- boundary-moving against secret assault -- or the four sexual-offense curses at vv.20-23).

boundary_rationale: Curse six opens the incest sub-series, recasting the case-law prohibition of MT 23:1 into performed form: oshb:Deut.27.20 אָרוּר שֹׁכֵב עִם אֵשֶׁת אָבִיו כִּי גִלָּה כְּנַף אָבִיו, closed by its own Amen. One legal category thus appears twice in the book, once as statute and once as curse, and the discrete closure marks the curse register's own unit here just as it does throughout the series.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A reviewer might merge all four incest-and-bestiality curses (vv.20-23) into one 'sexual purity' block given their shared theme; each instead names its own relationship and closes its own response, the same one-offense-per-unit logic applied to every other entry in the series.

A different class of victim is a genuine content distinction, offered here as color alongside the discrete-closure criterion that actually does the boundary work.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating this as inseparable from the surrounding incest curses as one undifferentiated sexual-purity block would submerge a real category difference (a different kind of victim entirely) and, more importantly, would abandon the response-formula criterion applied consistently elsewhere in the series.

The series' one-offense-per-response structure treats each named relationship as its own complete unit rather than clustering the whole incest theme into a single entry.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Combining this with the father's-wife curse as both concern incest within the immediate family is tempting on thematic grounds alone, but each is independently Amen-closed and names a different relationship, consistent with how every other pair of thematically adjacent curses in this series is kept separate.

parashah_two_witness: samekh after Deut.27.22

boundary_rationale: The ninth curse closes the four-entry incest run with a mother-in-law prohibition: oshb:Deut.27.23 אָרוּר שֹׁכֵב עִם חֹתַנְתּוֹ, closed by its own Amen, before the series returns to non-sexual social-order offenses at v.24. Nothing in this series grants special aggregating treatment to sexual offenses as opposed to any other class.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Keeping the whole incest run (vv.20-23) as one four-curse block is the recurring objection to this whole cluster of decisions; the same per-offense, per-response granularity is applied here as everywhere else in the series rather than singling out the incest curses for merger.
boundary_evidence_refs: oshb:Deut.27.23 אָרוּר שֹׁכֵב עִם חֹתַנְתּוֹ וְאָמַר כָּל הָעָם אָמֵן
parashah_two_witness: samekh after Deut.27.23

boundary_rationale: Secret murder reopens the social-order theme at curse ten, after the incest run: oshb:Deut.27.24 אָרוּר מַכֶּה רֵעֵהוּ בַּסָּתֶר, closed by its own Amen. Thematic echoes of the justice-for-the-vulnerable curse three entries earlier do not override the liturgy's even-handed performance structure, which grants every entry, near or distant neighbor alike, its own opening and its own response.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Reading this as thematically resuming the vulnerable-protection curses of vv.17-19 rather than as a fresh entry misreads the series' own logic: every curse opens and closes on identical terms regardless of which earlier entry it happens to echo.

parashah_two_witness: samekh after Deut.27.24

boundary_rationale: Judicial bribery, the eleventh curse, closes on its own Amen: oshb:Deut.27.25 אָרוּר לֹקֵחַ שֹׁחַד לְהַכּוֹת נֶפֶשׁ דָּם נָקִי. Deuteronomy's own separate treatments of bribery (16:19) and premeditated murder (19:11-13) confirm the book does not conflate this offense with the secret-murder curse just before it, supporting -- as color, not as the primary ground -- the same discrete-unit reading the response formula already requires.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Pairing this with the secret-murder curse as one 'unlawful killing' cluster is tempting on surface content, but bribery-driven judicial killing and covert personal murder are distinct offenses in this code's own case law, and each closes its own complete response regardless.
boundary_evidence_refs: oshb:Deut.27.25 אָרוּר לֹקֵחַ שֹׁחַד לְהַכּוֹת נֶפֶשׁ דָּם נָקִי וְאָמַר כָּל הָעָם אָמֵן
oshb:Deut.16.19 / Deut.19.11-13 (bribery and premeditated murder treated as separate cases elsewhere)
parashah_two_witness: samekh after Deut.27.25

boundary_rationale: The twelfth and final curse shifts register from a named act to a blanket statement about the whole law, 'Cursed is he who doesn't uphold the words of this law by doing them' -- oshb:Deut.27.26 אָרוּר אֲשֶׁר לֹא יָקִים אֶת דִּבְרֵי הַתּוֹרָה הַזֹּאת לַעֲשׂוֹת אוֹתָם, matching v.15's אֲשֶׁר-frame rather than the participial core running through vv.16-25 -- the series' own deliberate closing bracket. This is also the strongest single marker anywhere in the series: a petuchah, the highest-class division recorded in this book, closes MT 27:26, confirming both this final unit and the whole twelve-curse liturgy's end before ch.28's mirrored blessing-and-curse heading opens.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Reading this final curse as continuous with the eleven specific-offense curses that precede it (vv.15-25; v.15 shares the asher-frame with v.26 while vv.16-25 are participial) would erase the shift from a named act to a whole-law summary that the poem's own diction marks (אֲשֶׁר-clause matching the opening frame at v.15, not another participle); the petuchah at its close, unmatched in strength anywhere else in this series, corroborates treating it as the deliberate capstone.
boundary_evidence_refs: oshb:Deut.27.26 אָרוּר אֲשֶׁר לֹא יָקִים אֶת דִּבְרֵי הַתּוֹרָה הַזֹּאת לַעֲשׂוֹת אוֹתָם וְאָמַר כָּל הָעָם אָמֵן

boundary_rationale: A shift into named bodily and mental affliction opens this span, 'Yahweh will strike you with the boils of Egypt' -- oshb:Deut.28.27 יַכְּכָה יְהוָה בִּשְׁחִין מִצְרַיִם, adding tumors, scurvy, madness, blindness, and confusion of heart, closing on the groping-at-noonday image before the property-and-family-loss wave opens v.30. The prior ground for this seam -- that יַכְּכָה יְהוָה marks a 'fresh sub-wave' at v.27 -- does not survive scrutiny: the identical verb opens MT 28:22 (inside the preceding decision's own span, treated there as one link in an undifferentiated chain) and recurs again at MT 28:28, still inside this very decision's own span, never itself treated as opening anything. The verb is retired as boundary evidence. What remains is a genuine content signal: vv.27-29 name a cluster of personal bodily and mental afflictions (boils, tumors, scurvy, itch, madness, blindness, confusion of mind) categorically distinct from the national-scale plague, drought, military defeat, and corpse-desecration imagery of vv.20-26. No Masoretic marker exists anywhere in this stretch (OSHB records nothing between MT 28:14 and 28:68), so, as with its neighbors on both sides, the seam rests on this content shift alone.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Merging back into M8-Deut-182 as one unbroken 28:20-29 catalog is a live alternative once the verb-recurrence claim is dropped, since no formula, marker, or addressee change exists at the 26/27 line either. The content shift from national disaster to personal affliction is kept as the deciding factor because the campaign treats comparable un-marked content turns as sufficient boundaries elsewhere in this same chapter (the foreigner-ascendancy image at v.43, the causal clause at v.47), so applying a different standard here for consistency's sake would itself be the inconsistency.

boundary_rationale: A fresh register opens on 'You will betroth a wife, and another man shall lie with her' -- oshb:Deut.28.30 אִשָּׁ֣ה תְאָרֵ֗שׂ וְאִ֤ישׁ אַחֵר֙ ישגלנה/יִשְׁכָּבֶ֔נָּה (ketiv/qere as printed) בַּ֥יִת תִּבְנֶ֖ה וְלֹא תֵשֵׁ֣ב בּ֑וֹ כֶּ֥רֶם תִּטַּ֖ע וְלֹ֥א תְחַלְּלֶּֽנּוּ, fronting the object before the verb with no Yahweh subject at all, cataloging loss of house, vineyard, ox, donkey, sheep, and children to captivity through v.34's 'you will be maddened by the sight your eyes see' (וְהָיִ֖יתָ מְשֻׁגָּ֑ע מִמַּרְאֵ֥ה עֵינֶ֖יךָ אֲשֶׁ֥ר תִּרְאֶֽה). The span is now drawn at 28:30-34 rather than through v.35: v.35 restores both the divine subject and the striking-formula that vv.30-34 pointedly lack -- יַכְּכָ֨ה יְהוָ֜ה בִּשְׁחִ֣ין רָ֗ע -- and returns to the disease register of the preceding decision, echoing MT 28:27's שְׁחִין and its verbatim closing clause אֲשֶׁר לֹא תוּכַל לְהֵרָפֵא. The prior attachment of v.35 to this span rested only on adjacency (v.35 'cannot stand alone and cannot read forward'), which is not itself a text signal under mesh-r2's rule that markers corroborate but text drives; content decides here, and v.35's content is 183's disease cluster, not this span's deprivation-and-loss catalog. v.35 is accordingly re-cut as its own decision, M8-Deut-254. No Masoretic marker exists anywhere in this stretch (OSHB records nothing between MT 28:14 and 28:68), so, as with its neighbors, the seam at 34/35 rests on this content contrast alone. The seam at 29/30 rests on the same kind of content contrast in reverse -- affliction imagery giving way to deprivation imagery -- but that contrast is one of content, not of grammatical subject: v.29, the verse immediately before this seam, already has no divine subject of its own (וְהָיִ֜יתָ מְמַשֵּׁ֣שׁ בַּֽצָּהֳרַ֗יִם כַּאֲשֶׁ֨ר יְמַשֵּׁ֤שׁ הָעִוֵּר֙ בָּאֲפֵלָ֔ה וְלֹ֥א תַצְלִ֖יחַ אֶת דְּרָכֶ֑יךָ וְהָיִ֜יתָ אַ֣ךְ עָשׁ֧וּק וְגָז֛וּל כָּל הַיָּמִ֖ים וְאֵ֥ין מוֹשִֽׁיעַ), so the Yahweh-subject/no-subject framing that distinguishes 183's affliction wave from this deprivation wave holds wave against wave, not verse against verse at the 29/30 seam itself.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Keeping v.35 folded into this span as a one-verse coda, per the prior treatment, is a live alternative and is what this campaign drew before re-examination: v.35 genuinely cannot stand as the opening of v.36's fresh יוֹלֵ֨ךְ ... מַלְכְּךָ֙ material, so attaching it somewhere is unavoidable. It is not kept here because the row's own strongest evidence for it -- the verbatim echo of 28:27's אֲשֶׁר לֹא תוּכַל לְהֵרָפֵא and the shared שְׁחִין vocabulary -- argues for grouping v.35 with the disease material it echoes, not with the property-and-family-loss catalog it is merely adjacent to; using 'it has nowhere else to go' as the ground for a merger is the same move mesh-r2 forbids when a marker is silent, applied instead to content, and the campaign should not reward it just because the alternative is a bare one-verse decision.

boundary_rationale: Verse 35 does not belong in the property-and-family-loss catalog it was previously read as closing, and it does not open the exile-to-unknown-nation material that follows either. It restores the divine subject and striking-formula that MT 28:30-34 conspicuously omit -- יַכְּכָ֨ה יְהוָ֜ה בִּשְׁחִ֣ין רָ֗ע עַל הַבִּרְכַּ֨יִם֙ וְעַל הַשֹּׁקַ֔יִם -- and the clause אֲשֶׁ֥ר לֹא תוּכַ֖ל לְהֵרָפֵ֑א, which stands mid-verse here (v.35 continues מִכַּ֥ף רַגְלְךָ֖ וְעַ֥ד קָדְקֳדֶֽךָ), repeats verbatim the clause that closes MT 28:27, with the same שְׁחִין vocabulary (בִּשְׁחִ֤ין מִצְרַ֨יִם֙ at 28:27, בִּשְׁחִ֣ין רָ֗ע here); no other verse in the יַכְּכָה יְהוָה series (28:22, 28:28) shares both the שחין term and the cannot-be-healed clause with this one. The content is a return to the personal disease register of the preceding decision (183, MT 28:27-29), not a continuation of the deprivation register of 28:30-34, so v.35 is treated as its own low-confidence unit rather than folded into either neighbor by adjacency. Forward attachment into v.36 is excluded on the same ground already established for 184: v.36 opens on the fresh verb יוֹלֵ֨ךְ ('he will lead you away') naming 'your king' (מַלְכְּךָ֙), a term occurring nowhere else in the chapter, a clean formal seam that has nothing to do with v.35's content. This decision does not revive the retired warrant of the old M8-Deut-185, which isolated v.35 on the claim that the recurrence of the verb יַכְּכָה יְהוָה itself marked a fresh sub-wave; that claim is false, since the same verb opens MT 28:22 and MT 28:28 without being treated as a boundary anywhere else, and 183 already retires it explicitly. The warrant here is content alone: the disease vocabulary and the verbatim echo of 28:27, not the recurring verb. No Masoretic marker exists anywhere in this stretch (parashah_two_witness records nothing between Deut.28.14 and Deut.28.68), so, like its neighbors on both sides, this one-verse decision rests on an unmarked content signal, priced at low confidence.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding v.35 back into M8-Deut-184 as a one-verse coda to the property-and-family-loss catalog (28:30-35) was the prior treatment and remains the main alternative. It is not adopted because its only textual support was adjacency -- v.35 cannot stand as the opening of v.36's fresh material, so it was attached to whatever preceded it -- while the verse's own content (a Yahweh-subject striking-formula naming שחין and repeating 28:27's cannot-be-healed clause verbatim) points the other way, back to the disease cluster of 183. A merger justified only by 'nowhere else to put it' is the same kind of non-signal mesh-r2 excludes when the absent party is a Masoretic mark; content should not be held to a lower standard than markers are. Merging forward with 183 (MT 28:27-29) was also considered and rejected: 183's own span already closes cleanly at v.29, corroborated by nothing more than the same absence of markers this decision shares, and v.35 sits two verses past that close with an intervening deprivation catalog (30-34) between them, so extending 183 backward through the gap would itself be an adjacency-only move of the same kind rejected above. A standalone low-confidence decision is the reading that does not manufacture false support in either direction.

boundary_rationale: A fresh אֵלֶּה-colophon opens the Moab covenant address, 'These are the words of the covenant which Yahweh commanded Moses to make with the children of Israel in the land of Moab' -- oshb:Deut.28.69 (=WEB Deut.29.1) אֵלֶּה֩ דִבְרֵ֨י הַבְּרִ֜ית אֲֽשֶׁר צִוָּ֧ה יְהוָ֣ה אֶת מֹשֶׁ֗ה לִכְרֹ֛ת אֶת בְּנֵ֥י יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל בְּאֶ֣רֶץ מוֹאָ֑ב מִלְּבַ֣ד הַבְּרִ֔ית אֲשֶׁר כָּרַ֥ת אִתָּ֖ם בְּחֹרֵֽב. The forward-reading is supported by a genuine structural precedent inside the book, corrected here: 4:44-49's own אֵלֶּה heading (אֵ֚לֶּה הָֽעֵדֹ֔ת וְהַֽחֻקִּ֖ים וְהַמִּשְׁפָּטִ֑ים אֲשֶׁ֨ר דִּבֶּ֤ר מֹשֶׁה֙ אֶל בְּנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל בְּצֵאתָ֖ם מִמִּצְרָֽיִם), followed by four verses of geographic and historical description (4:46-49), is not 'immediately' followed by the summons at 5:1 -- a petuchah closes 4:49 first (וְכָל הָ֨עֲרָבָ֜ה עֵ֤בֶר הַיַּרְדֵּן֙ מִזְרָ֔חָה וְעַ֖ד יָ֣ם הָעֲרָבָ֑ה תַּ֖חַת אַשְׁדֹּ֥ת הַפִּסְגָּֽה), and only then does 5:1 open with וַיִּקְרָ֣א מֹשֶׁה֮ אֶל כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל֒ וַיֹּ֣אמֶר אֲלֵהֶ֗ם. That correction makes the precedent stronger rather than weaker: in both places a petuchah stands between the אֵלֶּה heading block and the summons that follows it (petuchah after 4:49 at Horeb; petuchah after 28:69 here at Moab), so the petuchah after MT 28:69 stops being a counter-signal against forward reading and becomes part of the very pattern that supports it. Disclosed candidly: a setumah still precedes this verse (after MT 28:68), a real, if now lesser, counter-signal for reading 28:69 backward as ch.28's colophon rather than forward as ch.29's heading. That asymmetry -- petuchah after matching petuchah on the forward reading, against one setumah on the backward reading -- bears on confidence rather than on the boundary itself, since the decision already brackets this verse as its own singleton rather than annexing it to either neighbor; given the strength of the corrected 4:44-49/5:1 precedent, confidence is raised from low to medium. This verse is MT's own 28:69, the third WEB/MT chapter-line offset in this book, requiring dual citation across the seam.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A reader following MT's chapter division would read this verse as the closing colophon of the ch.28 curse material rather than the opening of ch.29's address; the setumah before this verse is a real counter-signal for that direction, and is disclosed here as such. It does not carry the day because the corrected 4:44-49/5:1 precedent -- heading block, petuchah, then summons -- is the stronger book-internal pattern for reading אֵלֶּה forward across a petuchah, which is why the verse is still bracketed on the forward side rather than reassigned.

boundary_rationale: A single-verse closing aphorism, “The secret things belong to Yahweh our God; but the things that are revealed belong to us and to our children forever” (הַנִּסְתָּרֹת לַיהוָה אֱלֹהֵינוּ וְהַנִּגְלֹת לָנוּ וּלְבָנֵינוּ עַד עוֹלָם), closes ch.29 on a distinct wisdom-register note rather than continuing the devastation scenario, before the return-and-restoration promise opens ch.30. strongest_rejected_alternative: A reviewer might read this as the final clause of the future-generations scenario, but its shift to gnomic, timeless wisdom register (“the secret things belong to Yahweh”) is a distinct rhetorical mode from the concrete narrated reaction that precedes it.
