boundary_rationale: Ch.30 opens on a fresh conditional, 'It shall happen, when all these things have come on you, the blessing and the curse... and you shall call them to mind' -- oshb:Deut.30.1 וְהָיָה֩ כִֽי יָבֹ֨אוּ עָלֶ֜יךָ כָּל הַדְּבָרִ֣ים הָאֵ֗לֶּה הַבְּרָכָה֙ וְהַקְּלָלָ֔ה אֲשֶׁ֥ר נָתַ֖תִּי לְפָנֶ֑יךָ וַהֲשֵׁבֹתָ֙ אֶל לְבָבֶ֔ךָ בְּכָל הַגּוֹיִ֔ם אֲשֶׁ֧ר הִדִּיחֲךָ֛ יְהוָ֥ה אֱלֹהֶ֖יךָ שָֽׁמָּה, promising restoration, curse-transfer to Israel's enemies, and circumcision of the heart, in one unbroken waw-consecutive-perfect chain (וְשָׁ֨ב v.3, וֶהֱבִֽיאֲךָ֞ v.5, וּמָ֨ל v.6, וְנָתַן֙ v.7, וְהוֹתִֽירְךָ֩ v.9) bound together by a return-and-obey refrain recurring at vv.2, 8, and 10, closing before the Torah-accessibility passage opens its own fresh declarative at v.11. This decision now absorbs the material previously split off as its own decision at v.7: nothing marks 30:7 as a fresh unit rather than the fourth of five identical chain links, and the transfer of curses to Israel's enemies is simply the next promise in the same sequence, not a new topic. Samekh closes the preceding unit at Deut.29.28 (MT) = web:Deut.29.29 -- this citation sits inside the non-identical web Deut.29.1-29.29 = mt Deut.28.69-29.28 segment and requires the dual label -- and petuchah, the strongest marker class, closes this one at Deut.30.10 (identical numbering in both traditions), with no site anywhere between; syntax and Masoretic tradition converge exactly.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting at v.7 on the reasoning that the curse-transfer clause is a distinct turn in the promise's logic was the prior reading; every other link in the same five-part chain would support an equally plausible split on the same logic (each verse introduces its own specific blessing), which is precisely why treating v.7 alone as a boundary while leaving vv.3, 5, 6, and 9 unsplit cannot be sustained -- the whole chain stands or falls together, and it stands as one unit closed by the petuchah at v.10.

boundary_rationale: A fresh declarative opens the accessibility passage, “For this commandment which I command you today is not too hard for you or too distant” (כִּי הַמִּצְוָה הַזֹּאת אֲשֶׁר אָנֹכִי מְצַוְּךָ הַיּוֹם לֹא נִפְלֵאת הִוא מִמְּךָ וְלֹא רְחֹקָה הִיא), denying that Torah requires heavenly or transoceanic retrieval, closing on “the word is very near you” before the climactic choose-life charge opens v.15.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A reviewer might fold this into the closing choose-life charge as its rhetorical preparation, but it makes a distinct, self-contained argument (accessibility, not choice) with its own closing formula (“that you may do it”) before the choose-life charge opens on a fresh imperative of its own.

boundary_rationale: Ch.31 opens the succession narrative on its own notice, “Moses went and spoke these words to all Israel. He said to them, I am one hundred twenty years old today” (וַיֵּלֶךְ מֹשֶׁה וַיְדַבֵּר אֶת הַדְּבָרִים הָאֵלֶּה אֶל כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל…בֶּן מֵאָה וְעֶשְׂרִים שָׁנָה אָנֹכִי הַיּוֹם), announcing his incapacity and Yahweh’s and Joshua’s roles, closing on “be strong and courageous” before the direct charge to Joshua opens v.7.
strongest_rejected_alternative: One farewell scene running from this address straight into the direct Joshua charge that follows has surface appeal; v.7’s “Moses called to Joshua” instead shifts the addressee from all Israel to Joshua specifically, a real change of recipient the text itself marks.

strongest_rejected_alternative: A reviewer could fold this into the farewell address as its natural continuation, but the shift to direct second-person address to Joshua specifically (“in the sight of all Israel” as witnesses, not addressees) marks a formally distinct commissioning act.

Call Joshua” (וַיֹּאמֶר יְהוָה אֶל מֹשֶׁה הֵן קָרְבוּ יָמֶיךָ לָמוּת קְרָא אֶת יְהוֹשֻׁעַ), narrating the pillar-of-cloud theophany at the Tent’s door, closing before Yahweh’s own apostasy-prediction speech opens v.16.

This people will rise up and play the prostitute” (וַיֹּאמֶר יְהוָה אֶל מֹשֶׁה הִנְּךָ שֹׁכֵב עִם אֲבֹתֶיךָ וְקָם הָעָם הַזֶּה וְזָנָה), predicting future covenant-breaking and Yahweh’s hidden face, closing before the Song-command opens fresh in v.19.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A reviewer might read this as continuous with the Song command that follows since both concern the coming apostasy, but v.19’s “Now therefore write this song for yourselves” opens a fresh imperative addressed to Moses with a distinct topic (a literary remedy), not a continuation of the prediction itself.

strongest_rejected_alternative: A reviewer could split the command (v.19) from its rationale (vv.20-21), but v.20's 'For when I have brought them into the land' is the direct grounding clause for the command just given, one continuous instruction regardless of the citation correction.

boundary_rationale: A fresh fulfillment notice opens, 'So Moses wrote this song the same day, and taught it to the children of Israel' -- oshb:Deut.31.22 וַיִּכְתֹּב מֹשֶׁה אֶת הַשִּׁירָה הַזֹּאת בַּיּוֹם הַהוּא וַיְלַמְּדָהּ אֶת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל, reporting compliance with the command given in vv.19-21, and containing the sole 'that day' temporal marker in this pair of verses. Formerly grouped with v.23 as one merged narrator-report unit; the merge's own stated grounds (a shared 'same day' frame and uniform third-person report) do not hold once checked against the Hebrew -- v.23 carries no temporal phrase and opens its own introducing formula rather than continuing v.22's.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Keeping vv.22-23 together as one compact closing beat, on the reasoning that both fall within the same narrative moment, was the prior reading; it required treating v.23 as uniform third-person report about Moses, but v.23's own first-person oath language ('I will be with you... which I swore to them') is not narration about Moses at all, which is the deeper problem the temporal-frame and introducing-formula errors were both symptoms of.

boundary_rationale: A fresh command-plus-speech formula opens, 'He commissioned Joshua the son of Nun, and said, Be strong and courageous' -- oshb:Deut.31.23 וַיְצַ֞ו אֶת יְהוֹשֻׁ֣עַ בִּן נ֗וּן וַיֹּאמֶר֮ חֲזַ֣ק וֶֽאֱמָץ֒ כִּ֣י אַתָּ֗ה תָּבִיא֙ אֶת בְּנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל אֶל הָאָ֖רֶץ אֲשֶׁר נִשְׁבַּ֣עְתִּי לָהֶ֑ם וְאָנֹכִ֖י אֶֽהְיֶ֥ה עִמָּֽךְ. A sweep of every וַיְצַו in Deuteronomy -- 27:1 (וַיְצַ֤ו מֹשֶׁה֙ וְזִקְנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל אֶת הָעָ֖ם לֵאמֹ֑ר שָׁמֹר֙ אֶת כָּל הַמִּצְוָ֔ה אֲשֶׁ֧ר אָנֹכִ֛י מְצַוֶּ֥ה אֶתְכֶ֖ם הַיּֽוֹם), 27:11 (וַיְצַ֤ו מֹשֶׁה֙ אֶת הָעָ֔ם בַּיּ֥וֹם הַה֖וּא לֵאמֹֽר), 31:10 (וַיְצַ֥ו מֹשֶׁ֖ה אוֹתָ֣ם לֵאמֹ֑ר מִקֵּ֣ץ שֶׁ֣בַע שָׁנִ֗ים בְּמֹעֵ֛ד שְׁנַ֥ת הַשְּׁמִטָּ֖ה בְּחַ֥ג הַסֻּכּֽוֹת), and 31:25 (וַיְצַ֤ו מֹשֶׁה֙ אֶת הַלְוִיִּ֔ם נֹ֥שְׂאֵ֛י אֲר֥וֹן בְּרִית יְהוָ֖ה לֵאמֹֽר) -- shows every one of them continuing with לֵאמֹר; 31:23's וַיְצַו...וַיֹּאמֶר pairing is the only one in the book that does not. That formula is unique, not shared with 31:7's structurally different וַיִּקְרָ֨א מֹשֶׁ֜ה לִֽיהוֹשֻׁ֗עַ וַיֹּ֨אמֶר אֵלָ֜יו (a call-plus-speech, not a command-plus-speech), and its uniqueness strengthens rather than weakens the case for a fresh address here: a formula found nowhere else in the book marks this moment as distinct from the book's own command-giving pattern, not merely as a repetition of it. The genuine link to 31:7 is not the introducing verb but the commissioning speech itself -- both address Joshua directly with חֲזַ֣ק וֶאֱמָץ֒ כִּ֣י אַתָּ֗ה ... The speaker is best read as Yahweh rather than Moses: אֶהְיֶ֥ה עִמָּֽךְ ('I will be with you') and אֲשֶׁ֣ר נִשְׁבַּ֣עְתִּי לָהֶ֑ם echo v.21's אֲשֶׁ֥ר נִשְׁבָּֽעְתִּי almost verbatim, first-person oath language this book gives to Yahweh, never to Moses speaking of himself. No temporal phrase ties this verse to v.22's 'that day'; the two verses share adjacency but not grammar.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Reading v.23 as Moses's own continued narrated action (grouped with v.22 under a single narrator-report label) was the prior treatment; it cannot be sustained once the verse's first-person oath content is taken seriously, since the book nowhere else puts such language in Moses's own mouth.

boundary_rationale: The opening is genuine but was misdescribed: v.19's וַיַּ֥רְא יְהוָ֖ה וַיִּנְאָ֑ץ ('Yahweh saw and abhorred') does not make Yahweh the grammatical subject for the first time since the poem opened -- Yahweh is already the explicit subject at v.12 (יְהוָ֖ה בָּדָ֣ד יַנְחֶ֑נּוּ וְאֵ֥ין עִמּ֖וֹ אֵ֥ל נֵכָֽר) and the implicit third-masculine-singular subject of the wilderness-care sequence around it (יִמְצָאֵ֨הוּ֙ בְּאֶ֣רֶץ מִדְבָּ֔ר וּבְתֹ֖הוּ יְלֵ֣ל יְשִׁמֹ֑ן יְסֹֽבְבֶ֨נְהוּ֙ יְב֣וֹנְנֵ֔הוּ יִצְּרֶ֖נְהוּ כְּאִישׁ֥וֹן עֵינֽוֹ). What is genuinely distinctive at v.19 is that it resumes wayyiqtol narration with Yahweh as subject immediately after the second-person accusation that closes the historical recital -- צ֥וּר יְלָדְךָ֖ תֶּ֑שִׁי וַתִּשְׁכַּ֖ח אֵ֥ל מְחֹלְלֶֽךָ at v.18 -- and that resumption introduces the quoted divine speech. The closing edge is corrected: the quoted speech opened by וַיֹּ֗אמֶר אַסְתִּ֤ירָה at v.20 runs in unbroken first-singular forms (אַסְפֶּ֥ה, אֲשַׁלַּח, אָמַ֖רְתִּי) through v.27's וְלֹ֥א יְהוָ֖ה פָּעַ֥ל כָּל זֹֽאת, so the WEB stanza mark after v.22 previously used to close this span sits inside a single continuous quotation rather than at its edge, and cannot be the boundary's evidence under the rule that translation typesetting is metadata only. This span now absorbs the material previously split off as M8-Deut-218: nothing distinguishes v.23's אַסְפֶּ֥ה עָלֵ֨ימוֹ֙ רָע֔וֹת as a fresh strophe-opener from the vengeance material immediately before it -- same first person, no new subject, no vocative, no particle. The real formal seam is one strophe later, at 27/28, where v.28's כִּי ג֛וֹי אֹבַ֥ד עֵצ֖וֹת הֵ֑מָּה וְאֵ֥ין בָּהֶ֖ם תְּבוּנָֽה drops out of Yahweh's first-person voice into third-person reflection on the enemies -- exactly where the following decision (M8-Deut-219) already opens. Disclosed for the whole Song: MT carries no pe or samekh anywhere inside 32:1-43 (parashah_two_witness.json's nearest sites are petuchah after Deut.31.30 before and petuchah after Deut.32.43 after), so every internal seam in this poem, including this one, rests on text signal alone -- discourse frame and speaker change, not layout.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Keeping the prior two-decision split at 22/23, with the WEB \b mark as its stated evidence, cannot stand once that mark is treated as metadata rather than a driver: the Hebrew shows one uninterrupted first-person divine speech from v.20 to v.27, and merging is the only reading consistent with the mesh-r2 rule that translation stanza breaks never drive a boundary on their own.

The span is narrowed from its prior 34-38 extent: the Hebrew turns again at v.36, from Yahweh's first-person vengeance oath to third-person predication about him -- כִּֽי יָדִ֤ין יְהוָה֙ עַמּ֔וֹ. boundary_rationale: The poem's own theophany exordium opens on 'Yahweh came from Sinai, and rose from Seir to them. He shone from Mount Paran' -- oshb:Deut.33.2 וַיֹּאמַ֗ר יְהוָ֞ה מִסִּינַ֥י בָּא֙ וְזָרַ֤ח מִשֵּׂעִיר֙ לָ֔מוֹ הוֹפִ֨יעַ֙ מֵהַ֣ר פָּארָ֔ן וְאָתָ֖ה מֵרִבְבֹ֣ת קֹ֑דֶשׁ מִֽימִינ֕וֹ אשדת אֵ֥שׁ דָּ֖ת לָֽמוֹ, closing on 'when the heads of the people were gathered, all the tribes of Israel together' (v.5) -- a fitting close to the introit before the tribal sayings begin. The prior rationale claimed the per-tribe 'About X he said' formula itself opens at v.6; checked directly, v.6 (Reuben's saying) carries no introducing formula at all -- יְחִ֥י רְאוּבֵ֖ן וְאַל יָמֹ֑ת וִיהִ֥י מְתָ֖יו מִסְפָּֽר opens with a bare jussive, third-person about Reuben rather than to him. The formula device does not actually begin until v.7's וְזֹ֣את לִֽיהוּדָה֮ וַיֹּאמַר֒. The seam at 5/6 is retained on a narrower ground than before: the collective assembly notice of v.5 gives way to individually named reference starting at v.6, and v.6 is also the poem's first jussive, a shift in verbal mood as well as reference. This is priced honestly as a thin signal. The seam carries no Masoretic mark of any kind: the first section mark anywhere in ch.33 falls only after 33:6, so MT groups 33:1-6 as a single paragraph against the cut this decision draws, and the per-tribe formula that defines the series being opened is, by this decision's own finding, absent from v.6 -- the very verse the cut assigns to that series. What remains is one positive signal (collective-to-individual reference, reinforced by the mood shift to a jussive) working against an MT grouping and a formula gap at the seam's near edge, a weaker configuration than the campaign has priced above low elsewhere in this book: M8-Deut-244 sets low where a real formula is crossed by a single internal samekh, and M8-Deut-037 holds low where a real waw-chain is crossed by several internal samekh sites. A thinner signal, crossed by an actual MT grouping rather than by internal marks alone, does not price higher than either, so confidence is lowered from medium to low.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending this exordium through the Reuben saying (v.6) as one continuous opening movement is a live alternative once the false formula-claim is dropped, since v.6 genuinely lacks the device that marks every later saying; the collective-to-individual reference shift at v.5/6 -- the assembly named as one body in v.5 versus a single tribe named for the first time in v.6, spoken about rather than addressed -- is kept as the operative signal instead, consistent with the twelve tribal-saying decisions that follow it.

boundary_rationale: The tribal-sayings sequence opens on Reuben, 'Let Reuben live, and not die; nor let his men be few' -- oshb:Deut.33.6 יְחִי רְאוּבֵן וְאַל יָמֹת וִיהִי מְתָיו מִסְפָּר, the first of the individually addressed sayings, with (from v.7 onward) an explicit 'About X he said' introducing formula the poem repeats. Correcting a count carried in the prior rationale: this is not 'the first of twelve sayings.' Working through ch.33, the poem gives ten sayings for twelve tribes -- Zebulun and Issachar share one saying (vv.18-19), Joseph's saying (vv.13-17) covers both Ephraim and Manasseh without a saying of their own, and Simeon receives no saying at all. The boundary is unaffected; the count in the descriptive prose is fixed.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating all the tribal sayings as one undivided poetic register, as a repeated-template list might be merged elsewhere in this book, is not supported here: each saying (or paired saying) addresses genuinely different content -- life-and-numbers for Reuben, priestly office for Levi, agricultural abundance for Joseph -- matching this campaign's real-content-variance standard for splitting a register, regardless of the corrected count of how many such sayings there are.

strongest_rejected_alternative: A reviewer could group this with the Dan saying as a pair of brief northern-tribe blessings, but each opens its own “About X he said” formula and each names a distinct territorial or characterological blessing, the poem’s consistent per-tribe unit.

boundary_rationale: The per-tribe formula runs its final instance here, 'About Asher he said, Asher is blessed with children. Let him be acceptable to his brothers' -- oshb:Deut.33.24 וּלְאָשֵׁר אָמַר בָּרוּךְ מִבָּנִים אָשֵׁר יְהִי רְצוּי אֶחָיו, promising iron-and-bronze bars and strength matching his days, closing before v.26's אֵין כָּאֵל יְשֻׁרוּן drops the וּלְ...אָמַר pattern entirely and turns to a universal address, closing the tribal-sayings sequence. Correcting a count carried in the prior rationale: this is not 'the twelfth and final individually named tribal saying.' As already corrected at M8-Deut-227, the poem gives ten sayings for twelve tribes -- Zebulun/Issachar share one, Joseph covers Ephraim and Manasseh without their own, and Simeon has none -- so Asher's saying is well short of a twelfth in sequence, not the poem's twelfth entry. The boundary itself is unaffected.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending the Asher saying through v.26 as part of one continuous close is excluded on formal grounds regardless of the count correction: v.26 abandons the וּלְ-name-אָמַר pattern entirely for a universal second-person address to all Israel, a real formal seam closing the tribal-sayings sequence, independent of how many sayings preceded it.

boundary_rationale: A fresh universal address closes the poem, “There is no one like God, Jeshurun, who rides on the heavens for your help” (אֵין כָּאֵל יְשֻׁרוּן רֹכֵב שָׁמַיִם בְעֶזְרֶךָ), returning to the whole nation (not one tribe) as addressee, closing ch.33 and the poem on “You will tread on their high places” before the death-of-Moses narrative opens ch.34.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A reviewer might read this doxology as simply the final tribal saying (implicitly for Israel-as-a-whole) continuing the per-tribe pattern, but it lacks the “About X he said” formula entirely, marking a deliberate formal shift from individual tribal address to a closing peroration for the whole assembly.

boundary_rationale: The book’s final colophon opens on “Since then, there has not arisen a prophet in Israel like Moses, whom Yahweh knew face to face” (וְלֹא קָם נָבִיא עוֹד בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל כְּמֹשֶׁה אֲשֶׁר יְדָעוֹ יְהוָה פָּנִים אֶל פָּנִים), recapitulating the signs-and-wonders theme from 4:34 and 26:8 one last time, closing the whole book on “in the sight of all Israel,” a retrospective evaluative note that could only be written after Moses’s death just narrated.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A reviewer might fold this into the preceding Joshua notice as one continuous closing unit, but its own fresh, explicitly retrospective formula (“Since then, there has not arisen”) marks a vantage point after the fact, evaluating Moses’s whole career rather than continuing the narrated installation of Joshua.
